Preparation for the shareholder vote begins well in advance of the annual meeting, as firms weigh procedural matters that require investor approval and solicit shareholder proposals. In the United States, for example, all shareholder proposals must be received at least 120 days prior to the planned release of meeting materials, which must be vetted by the firm with their acceptance or rejection subject to review by regulatory authorities. Meeting materials are compiled in what is referred to in the United States as a proxy statement, which includes management and shareholder proposals along with a detailed agenda for the annual shareholder meeting and voting requirements and deadlines. Proxy statements typically include background information such as board candidate credentials, company performance, policies, and procedures as well as board recommendations for or against all decisions, with management’s rationale for supporting or rejecting all proposals. Proxy statements are usually distributed to shareholders indirectly via a custodian in whose name shares are typically held on behalf of an investor. Custodial services provided by a bank or broker involve maintaining ownership records with a securities depository as well as managing the safekeeping, settlement, and reporting for securities held by investors who are the true or so-called beneficial owner of shares. In rare instances, beneficial owners themselves are the registered holders of equity securities, with their name directly reflected in company records as a shareholder.

Voting eligibility is limited to shareholders of record or those shareholders whose identity is confirmed by a securities depository or custodian as of the record date or predetermined cutoff date for voting eligibility. Shareholders of record may or may not be the current beneficial owners of the stock. For example, a broker may serve as custodian for shares owned by a client; the custodian’s name is listed on the stock certificates while the client is the beneficial owner of the shares. Since the record date is often 30 days or more in advance of the shareholder meeting, investors who have sold the stock after the record date remain eligible to vote, while those who purchase shares after the record date but before the shareholder meeting are not. Once shareholders are identified and receive voting information, they must analyze this information, decide, and cast their votes via a shareholder voting service prior to the voting deadline or cutoff date, which is typically earlier for those shareholders who vote by proxy than those who attend the shareholder meeting in person. Given the vast amount of information that portfolio managers must evaluate when exercising voting rights for large, well-diversified equity portfolios comprised of many issuers across multiple markets, institutional investors often engage proxy advisors to assist in the voting process. Proxy advisors play an important role in gathering information, benchmarking important corporate governance principles across issuers, making voting recommendations, and keeping records associated with exercising shareholder votes across investment portfolios, as described below.

Two proxy advisory firms, Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) and Glass Lewis, are dominant players in the US proxy advisory market with a combined 97% market share. Both firms work with institutional investors and publicly listed companies around the world, providing coverage for tens of thousands of corporate shareholder meetings annually across over 100 markets. Given the variety of jurisdictional corporate governance practices, proxy advisors assist institutional investors and asset managers in making informed voting decisions on their public shareholdings. For example, in its 2024 Shareholder Proposal and ESG-Related Issues Benchmark Policy Guidelines, Glass Lewis recommends investor support of proposals that clearly link the subject of the proposal to firm value enhancement or risk mitigation in cases where the company’s management and board have failed to address the issue. On the other hand, Glass Lewis tends to recommend against shareholder proposals that are likely to encroach on company management’s day-to-day business operations without materially enhancing value or mitigating risk.

In seeking to focus on resolutions designed to enhance firm value or mitigate risk where management has fallen short, proxy advisors seek to create consistent governance standards across companies and industries. While management proposals typically involve legally prescribed matters, shareholder proposals raised by investors may sometimes suggest that boards take action that would encroach on management’s day-to-day operation of the company. In their voting decisions, investors should consider whether such proposals have the potential to materially improve corporate value or mitigate risk. These types of proposals often involve measures seeking to strengthen a company’s environmental or social policies, as described below.

sections.title: Shareholder Proposals To Address Climate Risk

blocks.x: Following the adoption by global and US regulators of more stringent rules that prevent companies from excluding investor proposals—particularly those related to environmental, social, or ethical concerns—equity issuers have faced a growing number of shareholder proposals in these areas from socially responsible investment funds and public policy groups. These and other shareholders are actively seeking corporate governance changes via the equity voting process. As a result, 2023 saw a large increase in climate-related shareholder proposals among oil and gas producers directly involved in greenhouse gas emissions, as well as issuers indirectly involved in the industry. For example, ExxonMobil faced several climate-related shareholder proposals at its annual meeting, which included proposals on adjusted greenhouse gas emissions reporting, establishment of a Paris Climate Agreement (Scope 3) target, direct methane emissions measurement, and the establishment of a new board committee on decarbonization risk. In each case, the board recommended against the proposals, which failed to pass. Separately, the City of New York’s retirement plans introduced a shareholder proposal at JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 annual meeting seeking company disclosure within a year of the bank’s plan to align practices for lending and underwriting to oil and gas and power generation companies with 2030 absolute greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets. JPMorgan management recommended against voting for the proposal, citing existing company initiatives in support of the goal to provide “secure, reliable, affordable energy while promoting clean energy solutions and strategies to reduce the world's carbon footprint.” The proposal came to a vote but was rejected by investors, receiving the support of just 12% of shareholders who cast their ballots.

Despite the frequent rejection of individual shareholder proposals by investors, the equity voting process provides a forum for investors to raise specific matters and exert influence on firms to meet desired standards. While shareholder proposals are typically non-binding, those that are approved, or fail despite the support of a significant fraction of shareholders, cause investors to expect the firm to address the issue raised to avoid reputational harm or signal a lack of responsiveness to investor concerns. Market regulators often take measures to increase transparency and shareholder protection in the voting process. For example, the European Union changed how proxy voting is conducted via the Shareholder Rights Directive (SRD). These rules were established to improve voting processes and information flows among institutional investors. The SRD improved the voting process by:
• ensuring shareholders may receive immediate electronic confirmation that their votes have been received and further confirmation of how they were recorded and counted;
• enabling the remote exercise of voting rights, with standardized voting-related information available electronically; and

• enhancing duties of care and disclosure applicable to intermediaries across the voting chain (including proxy advisors). Beyond the shareholder proposals described in the earlier case study, timely and active engagement in the voting process are extremely important aspects of share ownership for many asset managers and asset owners. In some cases, investors delegate their votes to asset managers, while in others, they are actively engaged in the voting process as part of their investment policy. Investor voting should serve to help the board protect and enhance the value of investor capital. As demonstrated in the

following example, the voting process is a critical way for these investors to demonstrate their stewardship and governance principles to stakeholders through concrete voting policies focused on effective boards and shareholder protections at firms held in their investment portfolio.

sections.title: Norges Bank Investment Management (Nbim) Voting Guidelines

blocks.x: Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) oversees the investment of the Government Pension Fund Global, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund tasked with managing approximately NOK12,340 billion in assets at the end of 2022. NBIM outlines their voting guidelines on minority shareholdings in publicly listed companies around two fundamental pillars: effective boards and shareholder protection. In their voting guidelines, NBIM views effective boards as characterized by three elements:

1. Independence relates not only to the overall proportion of independent directors but also to the membership of key board committees, such as the remuneration committee, as well as separation of board chair and chief executive officer positions. 2. Board composition areas of focus ensure that board members can commit sufficient time to company board responsibilities; ensure that independent board members bring appropriate industry expertise to their board positions; and finally, ensure that board composition reflects appropriate diversity. 3. Boards should be accountable to shareholders with respect to the board nomination and election process, board decisions and conduct, and recruiting and paying the right CEOs appropriately. In their voting guidelines, NBIM outlines shareholder protection with the following three components:

1. NBIM has approval guidelines related to voting rights, shareholder meetings, and governing documents. Notably, NBIM does not support companies with unequal voting rights across differing share classes. 2. Reporting guidelines focus on issues associated with companies’ external auditors, quality and timeliness of company financial statements, and sustainability disclosures. 3. NBIM’s capital guidelines provide value creation expectations for corporate share issuance or M&A plans as well as any related party transactions.

Overall, investors expect the companies whose shares they hold to protect and enhance the value of their investment by mitigating and managing risks through pursuit and execution of business strategies that increase value of shareholdings over time. The equity voting process is designed to ensure that these governance goals are attained.
Question Set

1. Which one of the following statements about shareholder proposals is most accurate? A. Failed proposals receiving the support of many investors are often addressed to protect an issuer’s reputation and respond to investor concerns.

B. Since shareholder proposals are typically binding, firms must take specific action when they are approved by a majority of investors. C. Shareholder proposals are frequently dismissed by a firm’s management without providing a rationale for their rejection. Solution: Choice A is correct. Despite their failure to be adopted, shareholder proposals that receive significant investor support are often addressed by the issuer after such a vote. Choice B is incorrect as shareholder proposals are typically non-binding. Choice C is incorrect as market regulators typically require some justification for the rejection of shareholder proposals.

2. The primary goal of the corporate shareholder voting process should be to: A. ensure that the corporation’s management is focused on value creation. B. ensure that the corporation’s board is independent. C. ensure that the corporation’s board is accountable to shareholders. Solution: Choice A is correct. While corporate shareholder voting may include multiple objectives, the goal is to ensure that the corporation’s management is able to focus on improving the firm’s value for shareholders. Choices B and C are incorrect as both responses are only elements of creating an environment in which management can pursue value creation for shareholders.

3. A broker buys Apple shares on behalf of a client, and the stock certificates are listed in the broker’s name as of the record date for Apple’s next shareholder meeting. The broker then sells the shares after the record date but before the proxy voting deadline. Who has voting rights to the shares? A. The broker B. The broker’s client C. The new owner(s) of the shares Solution: Choice B is correct. Although the Apple shares are registered in the broker’s name, the broker is the custodian of the shares while the client has voting rights of the shares because these are owned as of the record date. Choice A is incorrect because custody of the shares does not provide the broker with voting rights. Choice C is incorrect because the new owner did not buy the shares before the record date.

sections.title: Summary: Equity Jurisdictions, Classes, And The Voting Process

blocks.x: • To access equity markets outside of their domestic jurisdiction, issuers may choose a dual listing, while investors may purchase depositary receipts representing a position in foreign shares denominated in domestic currency.

• Dual class share structures are used to address the interests of a firm’s existing shareholders prior to wider ownership versus new shareholders via differences in the distribution of economic and voting rights.

• The equity voting process involves the identification and solicitation of shareholder votes on management proposals, such as electing directors or selecting an auditor, as well as on shareholder proposals for consideration.

• Institutional investors may use the voting process to exert their influence over issuers and to demonstrate investor stewardship and governance principles in accordance with their investment policies, often engaging proxy advisors to conduct research and provide recommendations.

The following information relates to questions 1-4 Audrey Lake is the Chief Investment Officer (CIO) of Mid States University Management Corporation (MSUMC), an endowment fund overseeing the university’s investment portfolio. MSUMC invests a significant portion of the portfolio in publicly traded equities, and their public holdings are often scrutinized by university stakeholders with respect to companies’ track records on managing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues. One of Lake’s early actions as CIO was to create a set of shareholder voting policies for MSUMC to follow with respect to conversations about their portfolio companies. These guidelines were written after consulting with one of the dominant proxy advisory firms. The following points highlight some statements included within MSUMC’s voting policy guidelines.
• MSUMC invests in foreign equities through the purchase of depositary receipts (DRs).
• MSUMC has implemented a policy in which they will not purchase shares in a company with a dual class structure.
• MSUMC has instituted voting guidelines that include a statement about voting on shareholder proposals that, if passed, would likely encroach on management day-to-day operations of companies.
• MSUMC carefully considers their votes on all ESG-related shareholder proposals to ensure that they can effectively communicate their rationales for “no” votes to stakeholders when necessary.
1. Which type of DR would MSUMC most likely own? A. Unsponsored DR
B. Sponsored DR
C. Either type of DR

2. Which one of the following statements provides the most likely reason why MSUMC would place a ban on owning shares of companies with dual class structures? A. Dual class structures typically provide multiple classes of traded shares with unequal voting rights.
B. Dual class structures typically provide unequal cash flow rights to shareholders.
C. Dual class structures typically provide one class of untraded shares with superior voting rights to those of traded shares.

B. Management is already working on the issue underlying the proposal.

Solutions

1. Choice B is correct. MSUMC would prefer to own sponsored DRs because the holder of sponsored receipts retains shareholder voting rights. Choices A and C are incorrect because the depository bank retains the voting rights on the company’s shares in an unsponsored DR.

2. Choice C is correct. MSUMC is concerned with being able to vote meaningfully, so publicly traded shares that are unlikely to have sufficient voting power are not attractive for the endowment. Choice A is incorrect because dual class structures rarely allow both classes to be traded. Choice B is incorrect because MSUMC is more concerned with voting rights.

3. Choice C is correct. In general, a shareholder proposal that, if passed, would cause the board to encroach on management’s day-to-day operations is not appropriate unless the actions would have material and positive effects on firm value and/or risk mitigation. 4. Choice A is correct. A company’s proxy statement includes both management and shareholder proposals, including the company’s voting recommendations to shareholders along with the rationales for the recommendations. Choice B is incorrect because shareholder proposals, if passed, are typically not binding on the company. Choice C is incorrect because shareholder proposals are not frequently passed.

compare exchange, off-exchange, and over-the-counter equities trading
describe liquidity measures for a publicly listed security and calculate float and average daily volume
describe types of equity indexes

blocks.x: Public equity markets play an important role as a source of new ownership capital for growing or established companies as well as a venue for buying or selling existing equity securities. Like other financial markets, public equity markets are composed of primary markets in which issuers raise financing and secondary markets in which previously issued shares are traded. In addition to providing liquidity for investors to sell or buy outstanding shares, secondary equity markets play a key role in offering price discovery to investors as well as performance feedback to management and stakeholders. The relative ability to trade securities is affected by whether execution occurs via an order-driven exchange or is managed using a broker network on an over-the-counter basis. Investors assess market liquidity based upon transaction costs as well as execution speed and trade volume. Similar to other asset classes, equity market indexes are used to gauge market risk and return versus individual securities, create new investment products, and evaluate fund manager performance. These and other aspects of equity issuance and trading are covered in this learning module.

1. Which of the following is least likely to be a reason for a company to issue equity securities on the primary market? A. To raise capital B. To increase liquidity C. To transfer shares from public to private owners Solution C is correct. Issuing shares in the primary market often gives existing private owners the opportunity to sell shares to public investors rather than the opposite. A is incorrect as issuance of equity securities is likely to raise capital. B is incorrect as issuance of equity securities is likely to increase the liquidity of the company’s stock.

2. Which of the following statements best distinguishes secondary equity markets from primary equity markets? A. Primary markets include only first-time equity offerings, while follow-on offerings of new shares are considered secondary market transactions. B. Pre-existing private shareholders may take advantage of primary markets to sell shares, while secondary markets are only available to public shareholders who purchase shares after an initial public offering (IPO) or direct listing. C. Primary markets are most active when market prices are rising, while secondary markets are active in both rising and falling markets. Solution C is correct. Primary issuance of new shares is most active when prices are rising, while secondary markets are active under all market conditions. A is incorrect since follow-on offerings of new shares are considered primary issuance. B is incorrect since pre-existing private shareholders may sell shares in the primary or secondary market.

3. Which one of the following trade types is most likely executed on an off-exchange basis? A. Limit orders B. Market orders C. Block trades Solution C is correct. Block trades are a major source of off-exchange activity. A is incorrect as limit orders are typically executed on an exchange. B is incorrect because market orders are executed on an exchange at the best currently available price.

4. Which one of the following indirect costs of trading can be observed from a limit order book? A. Market impact costs B. Bid–ask spread costs C. Delay costs Solution B is correct. The limit order book for a stock provides quoted bid and ask prices from which the bid–ask spread can be observed. A and C are both incorrect, because neither of these indirect costs can be observed from the limit order book.

5. Which one of the following measures most correctly describes the proportion of a company’s shares exchanged on a given trading day? A. Average daily turnover divided by market float B. Average daily turnover divided by total shares outstanding C. Total shares outstanding divided by average daily turnover Solution A is correct. Average daily turnover reflects the number of shares traded daily over a specified period, and market float reflects the number of shares available to trade. Thus, average daily turnover divided by market float most correctly describes the proportion of shares exchanged per day. B is incorrect because not all shares outstanding may be freely traded, thus market float is utilized instead. C is incorrect because this ratio would describe the number of days required to turn over all shares given average daily trading volume.

6. Which weighting approach is typically used for broad-based equity market indexes? A. Price-based B. Market capitalization-based C. Based on fundamental factors Solution B is correct. Typically, broad-based equity market indexes are weighted by each stock’s market capitalization within the index. Hence, they offer a more accurate representation of the market's performance than price-based or fundamental factor-based weighting. A and C are incorrect because neither price-weighting nor fundamental factor weighting are typical for broad-based indexes. These are more likely for more narrow indexes covering smaller subsets of a market.
MARKETS
describe primary and secondary public equity markets and their functions

Primary Equity Markets Primary equity markets are markets in which an issuer often lists and sells a new equity security to investors to raise ownership capital. In some cases, primary equity markets may be used to transform existing private ownership stakes into public equity capital. On the other hand, secondary equity markets are markets in which existing publicly listed shares are subsequently traded. As described in an earlier lesson on corporate issuers, firms may go from private to public ownership via an initial public offering (IPO) or, less commonly, via a special purpose acquisition company or a direct listing. A direct listing involves the listing of already issued and existing shares on an exchange at a price determined by the market without the use of an underwriter. For example, an IPO, described in earlier learning modules, involves a privately held firm entering the public equity market for the first time. These firms usually engage financial intermediaries known as investment banks to underwrite the sale of new shares to public equity investors. Equities may be sold via a public offering or a private placement, in which only a selected investor, or group of investors, may purchase the securities. Primary equity issuance usually involves a transfer from private to public ownership and may occur under the following circumstances:
• An early-stage firm seeks to expand beyond private founder and venture capital financing to attract public equity investment.
• A new public company is created as a result of the divestiture or spin-off of a division or business line from an existing public company.

• A firm whose shares were previously listed returns to the public equity market after a multi-year period over which private owners have restructured the business. In other cases, a national or regional government accesses the primary equity market in a full or partial privatization to transfer part or all of an existing government-held corporation to public investor ownership, as in the following example.

Hidroelectrica, a Romanian hydropower company, successfully completed an IPO in July 2023, raising over 9 billion Romanian leu (RON). While Hidroelectrica continues to be primarily owned by the Romanian government with a stake of approximately 80%, the IPO was initiated by the Bucharest Stock Exchange listing of a minority shareholder stake by Fondul Proprietatea SA (FP), a publicly traded investment fund with stakes in several government-owned companies. FP was established in 2005 to compensate expropriated property owners during
the Communist era in Romania. Following the IPO, Hidroelectrica became the fourth-largest weighting on the Bucharest Stock Exchange as well as the largest Romanian company traded on the exchange.

Regardless of a prospective equity issuer’s circumstances, size, or targeted investor base, the primary issuance process involves fulfilling listing and other regulatory requirements as well as soliciting potential investors for new publicly listed shares. Documentation: The creation and approval of an equity prospectus is a key IPO requirement. This offering memorandum describes the company and its business model, key industry and business risks, audited financial statements, and such details as the number of shares to be issued, expected price range, timetable, and use of issuance proceeds. Marketing: The issuer, its management, and advisers conduct a parallel process in which they introduce the company to equity analysts and prospective investors, gauging market acceptance and establishing demand as well as a price range for the prospective issuance. In contrast to the fixed-income book building process that often occurs on the day of issuance, equity issuers and their advisers usually spend much more time educating prospective investors about their business model, business risks, and the use of proceeds as well as establishing an offering price. Equity underwriters tend to have IPO pricing incentives that conflict with those of firm owners seeking to maximize the value of their business. Although underwriters may generate higher fees with a higher offer price, they often benefit even more from placing underpriced shares with preferred institutional investors identified as part of the book building process. Underpriced shares in IPOs provide incentives for investors to repeatedly seek allocations as new issuers come to the IPO market in hopes of securing attractive returns. As a result, underwriters are less likely to seek the highest offer price for issuers as this pricing behavior will reduce investor demand. This mispricing typically results in a commonly observed first trading day jump in the price of newly traded IPOs, as described below.

sections.title: Ipo Underpricing And Its Impact On Issuers And Investors

blocks.x: American academic Jay Ritter has conducted extensive studies on US IPOs. Using data from 1980 to 2023, Ritter documents the average underpricing (as measured by the percentage stock price increase on the first day of trading compared to the offering price) of over 9,000 IPOs at approximately 20%. Across all these IPOs,

this underpricing translates into USD233 billion of additional proceeds that could have hypothetically been raised by corporate issuers based upon the first trading day’s closing price. While underpricing has also been observed globally, it is not consistent across all issuers. For example, in 2020, average underpricing in US IPOs was over 40%, but almost 22% of IPO issuers in 2020 experienced negative first-day returns, indicating that the IPOs were overpriced. Why are IPOs underpriced? First, Ritter argues that underwriters have an incentive to underprice IPOs to generate demand among clients given the attractive first-day returns, especially for so-called “hot” IPOs, which are expected to generate significant investor demand. IPO underwriters also run full-service brokerages that charge fees and commissions. Investor clients are more willing to accept these fees and commissions if they receive preferential access to IPO allocations in return. Why are corporate issuers willing to accept lower IPO proceeds? Ritter suggests that company managers view first-day returns as a tangible increase in their own wealth based on their holdings of existing company stock. At the same time, the net proceeds not realized due to underpricing are an opportunity cost to the overall firm. These managers typically place a greater value on the positive first-day return versus the opportunity loss from lower IPO proceeds— another example of the principal and agent problem, where the principal is the shareholder and the agent is the manager.

A less common form of primary equity issuance involves the use of a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC). SPACs are created and exist solely for the purpose of raising capital to acquire an unspecified private company within a pre-agreed time frame, typically two years. These shell companies raise equity via an IPO and immediately place net proceeds in a trust account. The IPO proceeds may only be disbursed to complete an acquisition of a private company approved by shareholders (known as a de-SPAC transaction) within the contractual time frame or must be returned to investors.

sections.title: The Rise And Fall Of Spac Issuance

blocks.x: While blank check companies or SPACs offer public market investors the opportunity to invest together with celebrities, successful entrepreneurs, or private equity companies in an unspecified company, SPAC issuance is highly episodic. According to Jay Ritter, of the nearly USD300 billion raised by SPACs in the United States since 1990, over 70% of these proceeds were raised in 2020 or 2021 in just over 860 IPOs. Far fewer such deals were completed in Europe over the same period given restrictions on sales to non-professional investors. At the end of the two-year contractual time frame, SPACs must either complete a business combination approved by shareholders, extend the contractual deadline, or dissolve the company and return net proceeds to investors. As of mid-2023, nearly a third of SPACs created over this period had been liquidated. Others entered business combinations to convert early-stage or speculative private companies into public companies. One example of a successfully completed de-SPAC transaction involves Diamond Eagle Acquisition Corporation, a SPAC created by media executive Jeff Sagansky and former MGM CEO Harry Sloan. Within a year of its USD400 million IPO in May 2019, Diamond Eagle partnered with Europe-based SBTech to acquire DraftKings, Inc., a private US-based fantasy sports and betting company established in 2012 to capitalize on the growing legalization of sports gambling, which is now listed on NASDAQ as DKNG.

Other less common forms of primary equity issuance include a back door listing or direct listing. A back door listing involves the acquisition of a public company by a private firm to take advantage of an existing listing. Direct listings, described earlier, are usually limited to a few large private firms already familiar to investors, as in the following example.

Roblox, a gaming platform popular with children, experienced rapid growth in users as the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020. The company capitalized on this growth with plans to go public through a traditional IPO in late 2020. However, Roblox decided against this plan given the significant amount of underpricing observed in other high-demand IPOs. Roblox’s CEO sought to take the company’s shares public through a process that would improve outcomes for existing investors, including company employees looking to sell their shares in the public offering. In January 2021, Roblox received USD29.5 billion in new financing from two private investment firms at USD45 per share. The company then went public through a direct listing about two months later, and shares were offered to existing shareholders. Roblox’s shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on 10 March 2021 at a price of USD64.50 per share, and the stock closed at USD69.50 on its first day of public trading.

In contrast to the first-time offerings described above, a seasoned equity offering (or follow-on offering) involves the sale of additional units of a previously issued equity security. While this sale of new shares also requires a prospectus, it is typically an accelerated issuance process given greater market familiarity with the existing issuer. A follow-on offering may be dilutive or non-dilutive to existing shareholders, as shown in the following example.
Following the IPO in May 2012 at an offer price of USD38 per share, Facebook offered an additional 70 million shares to the public at USD55.05 per share, of which:
• 27 million shares were newly issued, and

• 43 million shares were from existing shareholders. As a result, Facebook’s seasoned offering included both dilutive and non-dilutive components. That is, the 27 million new shares issued by Facebook were a source of dilution for existing shareholders.

As shown in the example, a dilutive follow-on offering, also referred to as a primary follow-on offering, involves the sale of new shares that decreases each existing share’s proportional claim to the firm’s net income and assets. This approach is used by firms to raise additional equity capital for investment purposes and/or to reduce debt. A non-dilutive or secondary follow-on offering, in contrast, involves the sale of existing shares privately held in the public market for the first time, which does not change an existing shareholder’s proportional claim to the firm’s net income and assets under liquidation. Non-dilutive offerings allow firm founders and private investors to reduce their concentrated share ownership positions and diversify their equity holdings.

Secondary Equity Markets Secondary equity markets facilitate the trading of previously issued public equity securities. In contrast to primary markets, which are most active when prices and valuations are rising, the ability to buy and sell outstanding equity shares is equally important in both rising and falling markets, as described in the following case study.

Secondary Equity Market Resilience under Volatile Conditions 2020 was a tumultuous year in financial markets due to the global COVID-19 pandemic and the economic impact of social and government policy changes throughout the year. Using the S&P 500 Index as a measure of equity market performance, analysts may consider the 18.4% increase in 2020 as a relatively strong year for equities, as shown in Exhibit 2.

For example, as the economic impact of travel restrictions and shutdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic became apparent, the S&P 500 lost over a third of its value from late February to late March of that year. As seen in Exhibit 2, it was also a period of above average secondary market trading volume. Following the initial bear market, government policies in the form of both fiscal stimulus and monetary policy easing provided a significant boost to equity markets, which ended the year over two-thirds higher in price from the March 2020 low. Strong S&P 500 performance in 2020 was not equally distributed across sectors. Remote work policies, online shopping, and the closure of public spaces benefited shares in the Information Technology and Consumer Discretionary sectors, the two strongest sectors with 2020 returns of more than 47% and 34%, respectively. The worst-performing sectors were Energy and Passenger Airlines. While reduced demand drove a sharp drop in oil prices, travel restrictions and lockdowns caused consumer travel demand to plummet, leading to share price declines in both sectors of roughly a third through 2020.

Beyond the ability to readily trade shares, secondary markets offer critical price discovery and other benefits to investors, issuers, company stakeholders, and other market participants. For example, observed market prices allow investors to assess periodic share return, and they serve as a basis for comparison for financial analysts seeking to estimate share value using equity valuation techniques (described in detail later). Issuers and firm stakeholders use secondary market prices as an important gauge of company performance. Investor access to current and historical price data for individual equities and equity indexes supports a variety of public market investment approaches. For example, investors can easily measure returns, volatilities, and correlations across time and construct equity portfolios with an efficient risk–return tradeoff. Public market data is a critical input in comparing an individual share’s performance over time to firms of a similar size, those in the same sector, or those with other common features as well as to the overall equity market using a broad-based index. In the case of issuers, secondary equity market prices provide valuable feedback to management and other stakeholders of the firm that supports decision making, potential financing, and compensation activity. For example, a publicly traded firm may consider a corporate restructuring plan to increase operating efficiency. These plans are often tied to expected share price improvements to demonstrate their anticipated value to shareholders. Firms seeking to either raise additional equity capital or distribute capital to shareholders are likely to factor secondary market pricing and trading as a consideration into their decision-making process. For example, a firm whose secondary market price is rising sharply is more likely to pursue a follow-on offering, while one with a depressed trading price may consider share repurchases in lieu of dividends as a form of shareholder distribution.

Firms that employ restricted stock units (RSUs) and other forms of share-based incentive compensation for directors and management use secondary market price changes to gauge performance. RSUs are shares rewarded to employees as part of a compensation package that are restricted from sale during a vesting period that may last several years. Once the vesting period has lapsed and the employee remains in good standing or has met certain requirements after leaving the employer, RSUs may be sold or retained as unrestricted shares.

Share-based compensation, including restricted stock units and options, has become a more important component of corporate pay packages over the years. According to Morgan Stanley, a US-based financial services firm, share-based compensation has grown from 0.2% to 1.3% of sales among companies in the Russell 3000 Index between 2006 and 2022. The current estimate of sharebased remuneration as a fraction of total compensation among these firms is approximately 6%–8%. Share-based compensation typically comprises a greater proportion of total compensation for smaller publicly listed firms as well as firms in the Information Technology sector. A significant rationale for this approach is to better align employee incentives with those of their employer. In addition, this approach replaces a portion of cash compensation and reduces the need to raise additional capital. Company shares used for compensation may either be issued as new shares or involve previously repurchased shares. Issuance of new shares is dilutive for existing shareholders, while repurchasing existing shares for compensation is less likely to reduce existing shareholder ownership. However, many smaller firms using share-based compensation do so to conserve cash, suggesting these firms lack the ability to pay cash to buy back shares. The executives and employees receiving such compensation are willing to place some of their pay at risk in exchange for expected share appreciation.

Beyond the direct effects on equity investors (the issuer and employees with share-based compensation), changes in a company’s market value based on secondary market share price movements are an important gauge of a company’s financial health for other stakeholders as well. These include suppliers, competitors, customers, salaried employees, and government policymakers. Given the large swings in the market’s perception of a company’s value over time, as shown in the case of GameStop in an earlier learning module, it is important for financial analysts to establish a view on a company’s value using equity valuation techniques. Equity valuation is covered in detail in later learning modules.

1. Which one of the following best characterizes an IPO? A. Primary market transaction B. Secondary market transaction C. Direct listing Solution A is correct. An IPO is best characterized by raising new capital through share issuance and is generally a primary market transaction. B is likely incorrect as an IPO is not usually used to trade existing shares, so an IPO is not typically characterized as a secondary market transaction.
C is incorrect because a direct listing is simply a specific mechanism for a company to issue new shares to public investors as an alternative to the IPO process.

2. Which of the following public equity offerings is likely most dilutive? A. An IPO in which proceeds are used to buy new assets B. An IPO in which all offered shares are currently owned by early-stage investors C. A seasoned offering in which all offered shares are currently owned by the company founder Solution A is correct. An offering in which new shares are offered to raise capital to accomplish an objective, such as buying new assets, is dilutive to existing shareholders. B and C are incorrect as both offerings involve no new shares, so these are likely non-dilutive offerings.

3. Which one of the following statements most correctly describes IPO underpricing? A. IPOs are typically priced below the stock’s intrinsic value. B. IPOs typically generate substantial long-run returns. C. IPOs typically experience a jump in price on their first trading day. Solution C is correct. On average, IPO offerings experience a significant one-day return equal to the difference between the offering price and the publicly traded price at the close of the stock’s first day of trading. This suggests the shares were sold at a discount to their first-day closing price, with this difference referred to as IPO underpricing. A is incorrect as intrinsic value must be estimated and cannot be directly observed to compare to the IPO price. B is incorrect because underpricing cannot be assessed based on favorable long-run returns because these reflect new information not knowable at the IPO date. Although long-run returns are variable, they cannot reliably predict underpricing.

Exchange Trading of Equities An equity exchange is a rules-based venue where market participants regularly trade equity securities. As in the case of other exchanges, trading rules designed to promote liquidity and transparency include the establishment of regularly scheduled trading hours each business day, during which an order matching system is used to link share purchase and sale orders, as shown in Exhibit 4.

Exchange-based trading activity is executed through firms that are members of the exchange and are registered as broker–dealers. These financial intermediaries either act on behalf of clients as an agent or serve as principal counterparty to a financial transaction with a client. In the case of exchange-traded equities, broker–dealers act as an agent for investors by bringing orders to the market via the exchange’s order management system. Equity trading orders of all types are typically entered in standardized share lots of a minimum 100 shares each. Stock exchanges also commonly designate a single dealer (or market maker) to ensure the orderly, continuous trading of each listed security. The role of this designated market maker involves purchasing, selling, or holding shares to promote liquidity and price discovery when the market opens and closes as well as at times of market imbalance or high volatility. These exchange rules, centralized systems, and standardization seek to promote a liquid trading environment for company shares, as measured by the explicit costs of trading, or out-of-pocket fees and commissions, as well as by implicit costs in the form of a bid–ask spread (or bid–offer spread):
Bid–ask spread = Lowest ask price – Highest bid price. | (1)

The bid–ask spread is the asking or offer price (price at which a trader will sell a specified quantity of a security) minus the bid price (price at which a trader will buy a specified quantity). This may be expressed in absolute currency terms, as in Equation 1, or as a percentage of the lowest ask price, as in Equation 2: (Lowest ask price – Highest bid price) Bid–ask spread (%) = ___________________________
Lowest | ask price   . | (2)
This spread is a common measure of the cost of purchasing and selling shares in the current market.

Exchange rules also facilitate the execution of different investor order types, such as market orders and limit orders. While a market order involves directing a broker to buy or sell a specific number of shares at the best available current market price, a limit order imposes restrictions on the sale or purchase of shares. That is, a buy limit order imposes the constraint of a maximum share price to be paid, while a sell limit order specifies a minimum price to be received. If these respective prices are not reached, the order is not executed. Exhibit 5 provides a graphical representation of a limit order book showing these relationships.

For a stock to trade on an exchange, it must be listed and continue to meet exchange listing requirements. Equity listing requirements typically include a minimum number of shareholders, minimum numbers each shareholder may hold, minimum book equity value or net worth and/or profitability levels, and a minimum percentage of stock that is publicly traded. A growing number of equity exchanges exist to accommodate smaller firms at an earlier stage of development, as described in the following case study.

sections.title: Toronto Stock Exchange (Tsx) Versus Venture Exchange (Tsxv)

blocks.x: LISTINGS

TMX Group, a Canadian-based financial company, includes two stock exchanges for different types of corporate issuers. For larger, more mature issuer companies, the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) is an appropriate venue for listing equity offerings and secondary market trading. In contrast, the TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV) is for early-stage and smaller issuer companies, many of which are in the development stage; while they meet alternative listing criteria, they often have yet to earn a profit. TSXV also has a much higher concentration of firms in fewer sectors, such as mineral exploration and technology, while TSX has a more balanced composition across sectors. Not surprisingly, TSX represents most of the market capitalization across the two exchanges. The total quoted market value of TSX companies is CAD3,792 billion in 2022 compared to CAD70 billion across over 1,700 companies listed on each of the respective exchanges. However, for companies raising capital, the differences are less extreme. The average size of equity capital raised is CAD50 million for TSX companies versus CAD4.4 million for TSXV companies. TMX Group has a streamlined process through which eligible issuers meeting more stringent TSX exchange requirements can “graduate” from TSXV to TSX, 16 of which completed this in 2022.

Off-Exchange Trading of Equities While standard trades of a small to moderate size are easily digested by the exchange, others may achieve better execution when directly executed with a broker–dealer. These equity trades typically involve illiquid shares, very low volume trades (often in low price shares) initiated by retail investors, or very large trade order sizes known as block trades. Block trades are a major source of off-exchange activity and are usually defined as an order of 10,000 shares or more for a specific issuer. In many cases, block trades are sent to a broker–dealer that either breaks the block into smaller individual orders executed over time to minimize the adverse price impact or sends them simultaneously in smaller pieces to multiple parties to achieve the same effect. In other cases, such as mutual funds, asset managers may agree to bilateral or multilateral exchanges of shares at a market closing price separate from an exchange order system. In most cases, off-exchange trading seeks to minimize the implicit costs of trading, which are the indirect and generally unobservable costs resulting from the market impact of trading. Implicit costs apart from the bid–ask spread arise from the following sources:

• Market impact (or price impact) is the cost of immediately executing a trade on transaction prices. Traders who want to fill large orders often must move prices to encourage others to trade with them.
• Delay costs (also called slippage) arise from the inability to complete the desired trade immediately. Traders fail to profit when they fill their orders after prices move as they expect.
• Opportunity costs (or unrealized profit/loss) arise from the failure to execute a trade promptly. Traders fail to profit when their orders are not executed, and prices move as they expect.

Over-the-Counter Trading of Equities In contrast to exchange-traded equity securities, over-the-counter (OTC) equity trading involves a network of broker–dealers who buy and sell shares among themselves rather than via a centralized trading system, as shown in Exhibit 6.

The OTC market is sometimes referred to as a quote-driven market. Shares traded on an OTC basis are typically those of firms that are smaller in size that either decide to forego the costs of registration on a larger domestic equity exchange or fail to meet the minimum listing requirements. In contrast to an electronic order-driven system in the case of exchange trading with a designated market maker as described earlier, a quote-driven trading system consists of multiple market makers, which are typically broker–dealers, that continuously show bid and ask prices to investors seeking to buy or sell shares. Rather than posting an order on a centralized trading platform, these market makers will typically either fill the investor’s order from their inventory of shares or seek to match an investor’s trading instruction with an offsetting order from another market maker or investor. Quote-driven market systems tend to offer the highest likelihood of trade execution under most market conditions, as a broker–dealer or market maker posts bids and offers and must execute at these prices when receiving orders. On the other hand, OTC markets offer less transparency than exchange-traded markets, as individual trades and orders are not readily visible to market participants. While trading among market makers tends to cause bid and offer prices to be similar across broker–dealers, buyers and sellers have no assurance that they are executing at the best available market price at a given time. OTC broker–dealers may also decide to provide less liquidity in times of market stress.

1. Which one of the following is most likely a minimum size of an equity trading order submitted on an exchange? A. 10 shares B. 100 shares C. 1,000 shares Solution B is correct. Equity trading orders submitted for exchange trading are typically entered in standardized share lots of a minimum 100 shares each.

2. Which one of the following is least likely to be an important part of an equity exchange’s minimum listing requirements? A. Number of shareholders must be greater than some minimum level B. Percentage of shares available to be traded publicly must be greater than some minimum level C. Company sales must be greater than some minimum level Solution C is correct. Company sales levels are least likely to be employed as a listing requirement as other fundamentals are likely more important (such as profitability). A is incorrect because exchanges are likely to require enough possible sellers of shares as represented by the number of shareholders. B is incorrect because exchange trading requires sufficient shares to be available for trading.
3. Which one of the following statements is most likely true of block trades? A. Block trades are typically traded on exchanges in their full order size.

B. Block trades are broken down into smaller sizes to minimize the bid– ask spread for the stock. C. Block trades are broken down into smaller sizes to minimize the price impact of the trade. Solution C is correct. In many cases, block trades are sent to a broker–dealer that breaks the block into smaller individual orders executed over time to minimize the price impact. A is incorrect because the larger size of block trades typically makes it impractical to trade all the shares in one order. B is incorrect as the bid–ask spread reflects both buy and sell orders. A block trade will only reflect a buy or sell order. The bid–ask spread is an explicit cost of trading, while block trades are typically broken into smaller orders to minimize the implicit costs of trading.
describe liquidity measures for a publicly listed security and calculate float and average daily volume

As in the case of other financial markets, equity market liquidity involves the relative ease with which market participants can buy or sell shares in terms of both cost and timing. The explicit and implicit costs associated with trading described earlier can vary widely based upon the size and timing of trade orders as well as the release of other new information affecting share prices, among other factors. An important quantitative measure of liquidity in terms of market turnover involves the relationship between market float and average daily volume. While market float is sometimes used to refer to the total market value of shares freely traded, we refer to the number of issuer shares that are available to freely trade in the public market: Market float = Total shares outstanding – Restricted shares or shares not available for trading.

The average daily volume reflects the average number of issuer shares traded each business day over a pre-determined period, shown below as n days: n ∑ (Shares traded per day)i verage daily volume = _____________________ i=1 A n . 	                                      (6) The ratio of average daily volume to market float gives an overall indication of the proportion of shares outstanding to be exchanged on a given trading day. This ratio is referred to as the turnover ratio: Average daily volume ________________ Turnover ratio = Market
float | . 	 | (7)

These liquidity metrics allow equity investors to compare their position in an issuer’s stock with the relative ability to liquidate a position based upon overall market activity. This comparison is particularly important for large positions in smaller publicly traded companies.
Knowledge Check

Eastern States Pension Plan owns 300,000 shares of Merlewis Corporation. The number of Merlewis shares outstanding is 1,250 million shares, with 80% of the shares representing the company’s market float. The average daily volume in Merlewis over the last month has been 1,500,000 shares. Eastern States internal trading guidelines prohibit the fund from buying or selling more than 8% of a stock’s average daily trading volume on any given day. The Chief Investment Officer of Eastern States has instructed the plan’s trading staff to implement a complete liquidation of the plan’s holdings in Merlewis shares.

1. Calculate the number of days necessary to complete the liquidation of Eastern States’ position in Merlewis shares. Solution Eastern States’ current position in Merlewis represents 20% of average daily trading volume (=300,000 ÷ 1,500,000). A complete liquidation of their holdings given the 8% constraint implies that Eastern States must sell their Merlewis holdings over at least three trading days. Dividing 20% by 8% gives an answer of 2.5. Thus, they cannot fully liquidate Merlewis shares in two days, but may complete the sale within three days.

Secondary equity market liquidity encompasses several measures beyond the transaction costs mentioned earlier and the proportion of shares traded per day, namely market depth, market breadth, and market resiliency, or a market’s relative speed of price adjustment. As described earlier, market depth refers to the relative size of orders posted that are at or very near the best currently available bid and offer prices, while market breadth is a measure of the number of orders at different price levels both above and below, but very close to the best bid and offer prices. The combination of market depth and breadth reflects the number, size, and dispersion of orders within a trading book. A high degree of depth and breadth ensures the ability to execute trades of a manageable size quickly and without significant market price moves under relatively stable market conditions. Using algorithms effectively to split large orders into smaller parts hinges on the market’s depth and breadth. This strategy facilitates smooth execution of trades without causing a significant adverse price impact. Market resiliency refers to the relative ability of an issuer's shares to maintain a stable market-clearing price, the price level at which all buy and sell orders for a security can be executed, leaving no excess demand or supply, and subsequently revert quickly to such a price following a market shock. Shocks affecting share prices cause an initial change, the impact of which may be dampened by greater market depth and breadth, as well as a period of convergence to a new market-clearing price. The speed of adjustment depends not only on existing orders, but also those not revealed by brokers, including orders with special conditions, block trades executed in smaller portions, or computer-based trades triggered by market moves. These unobservable forces can contribute to significant intraday share price volatility.
1. An equity market’s depth most correctly refers to: A. the market’s ability to absorb numerous trade orders.

B. the typical bid–ask spread observed for stocks trading in the market. C. the market’s ratio of market orders to limit orders. Solution A is correct. A market with greater depth has many orders at or near the best available bid and offer prices, providing traders with confidence that there are sufficient buyers and sellers to absorb numerous orders. B is incorrect. Market depth implies more about the limit orders below the highest bid price and above the lowest ask price. The size of the bid–ask spread is not indicative of market depth. C is incorrect as market depth does not refer to any specific ratio regarding market to limit orders. For an individual stock, a significant number of limit orders might be indicative of the market’s ability to absorb market orders. However, if all limit orders are close to the prices associated with the bid– ask spread, the market would have little depth.

2. Which of the following provides the most accurate estimate of the proportion of shares outstanding exchanged per day given the following information: A company’s number of shares outstanding is 1,250 million shares with 80% of the shares representing their market float. The average daily trading volume in the company’s stock over the last month has been 1,500,000 shares. A. 0.60% B. 0.12% C. 0.15% Solution C is correct. The ratio of average daily turnover to market float gives an overall indication of the proportion of shares outstanding exchanged on a given trading day. Daily turnover is given as 1,500,000 shares, and market float is 1,000 million shares (= 80% × 1,250 million); so, the ratio is 0.15% (= 1,500,000 ÷ 1,000,000,000). B fails to adjust for the fact that just 80% of shares outstanding represent market float by dividing average daily volume by total shares outstanding rather than those available to trade. A makes the error of dividing average daily volume by the 20% of shares outstanding that are restricted or privately held and therefore not included in market float.

3. Which one of the following statements most correctly describes the factors associated with share prices and market shocks? A. A stock with greater market resiliency is more likely to be able to avoid market shocks. B. Greater market depth and market breadth can dampen the initial price impact of a market shock. C. The speed of market price adjustment following a market shock is determined by the pre-existing market order book. Solution B is correct. Greater market depth and market breadth reduce the initial price change following a market shock.

A is incorrect because market resiliency does not help shares avoid price shocks; rather, it involves the ability of market prices to adjust to shocks. C is incorrect because unobserved trades, such as those orders not revealed by brokers and block trades, may also affect the speed of price adjustment. Average trading volume is likely to be a very small fraction of overall market float because of large numbers of shares outstanding for most publicly traded equities.
describe types of equity indexes

Market indexes support the tracking of risk and return, performance evaluation, and benchmarking investments and investment managers. They also form the basis for indexed investment strategies. Several features distinguish their composition and use in equity markets. Equity indexes are commonly comprised of a fixed number of constituents, each represented by the issuer’s common share outstanding. Each issuer’s market share price is used to determine the index value based upon the respective weighting methodology, which is typically based upon market capitalization, price, or other factors described below. The following case study illustrates the composition and determination of a major equity market index.

Established in 1997, the NIFTY 50 equity market index is comprised of 50 of the largest firms traded on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) of India. The index is calculated using a market capitalization–based weighting methodology that is float-adjusted, with the index value representing the total market value of all the stocks in the index relative to a base year value of 1,000 set in 1995. As of 2024, the largest component of the index was HDFC Bank, with over 13% weightage in the index; the smallest was UPL, a chemical company with an index weight of less than 1%. Financial services firms comprise over 30% of the NIFTY 50’s market value, followed by information technology (14%) and oil and gas (11%). NIFTY 50 constituents are subject to review and replacement on a semi-annual basis, with more frequent changes occurring because of a constituent delisting, merger, or other corporate action. With around two-thirds of total NSE market value and just over half of NSE trading volume comprised by its constituents, the NIFTY 50 is a broad-based reflection of overall Indian stock market performance and serves as the underlying for the world’s most actively traded equity derivative contract.

As in the case of the NIFTY 50 index described above, most broad-based equity indexes for a given market include the largest listed firms adjusted by market float and calculated on a market capitalization–weighted basis. Equity market participants commonly track and gauge equity performance across markets using these indexes, as shown in Exhibit 7 using the example of a Bloomberg World Equity Indexes (WEI) summary page.
