As Exhibit 8 demonstrates, numerous equity index types exist to meet the needs of market participants, including broad-based indexes, indexes with an industry sector focus, indexes based upon a specific investment theme, and indexes based upon alternative weightings using so-called fundamental factors (i.e., measures other than market capitalization that may incorporate an issuer’s revenue, earnings, dividends, or book value). Broad-based indexes are typically tiered based upon issuer size and often include specific indexes that track the performance of firms of different sizes. The most comprehensive equity market index is typically referred to as a composite equity index, which is typically one that includes securities representing more than 90% of the selected market’s value. Composite equity indexes are commonly broken down into indexes with fewer constituents based upon size to distinguish the performance of small-, medium-, and large-cap companies. For example, the constituents of the NIFTY 500 composite index are included in three smaller indexes: The NIFTY 100 is comprised of the largest 100 firms in the NIFTY 500, with approximately 75% of the composite index’s market capitalization. The NIFTY Midcap 150 includes those firms ranked 101–250, comprising 15% of composite index market value. The NIFTY Smallcap 250 includes the remaining small firms, which total 10% of index market capitalization. Despite the popularity of equity indexes based upon company size, several considerations give rise to a need for narrower, industry-based indexes. Broad-based capitalization-weighted index performance is heavily influenced by the fortunes of its largest firms (i.e., those whose shares have appreciated) and its firms in concentrated industries. Sectoral indexes facilitate a comparison of firms in the same business, allowing investor and issuer benchmarking across competitors, and supporting the creation of index-based investment products to allow investors to establish equity exposure to a specific industry rather than an individual company or the entire market. Investment themes, on the other hand, involve indexes created based on investor trends beyond selecting a certain industry or company size. Examples of NSE indexes based upon investment themes include the following areas:
• Firms whose activities are primarily focused on domestic sales in India (NIFTY India Consumption)
• Capital-intensive, long-lived assets used to provide essential services (NIFTY Infrastructure)
• Issuers screened to ensure compliance with Islamic law (NIFTY 50 Shariah)
• Issuers screened to ensure compliance with specific environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles (NIFTY 100 ESG) The following case study describes the screening process for an ESG index.
S&P EUROPE ESG 350 INDEX

The S&P Europe ESG 350 Index is constructed using the constituents of the underlying S&P Europe 350 Index, a market capitalization–weighted index that seeks to maintain a balanced representation across sixteen developed European markets as well as across global industries. First, several criteria for exclusion are applied to the constituents. For example, companies engaged in certain business activities deemed not in compliance with ESG principles, such as certain weapons, thermal coal, tobacco, oil sands, small arms, and military contracting, are excluded. Firms considered non-compliant with UN Global Compact Principles are also removed from consideration.

The remaining eligible constituents are ranked by their respective S&P DJI ESG score, a scoring methodology that seeks to measure ESG risk and performance factors for corporations, with the bottom 25% of firms excluded from the index, with a focus on financial materiality. This index is float-adjusted market capitalization weighted.

Indexes based upon alternative weighting methodologies have enjoyed greater popularity due to the perceived biases and shortcomings of standard market capitalization-weighted indexes. The simplest form involves an equally weighted index based upon the same constituents as a broad-based index based on market capitalization. For example, under the NIFTY 50 Equal Weight index, both the largest (HDFC Bank) and smallest (UPL) NIFTY 50 constituents would have a weight of 2%. This approach seeks to remove perceived biases of a greater weighting given to the largest companies and those whose prices have appreciated under a standard market capitalization-weighted method. Investor interest in so-called factor-based investing, or investment selection based upon fundamental factors believed to be underlying drivers of equity performance such as earnings growth and well-capitalized balance sheets, has been the catalyst for the creation of other indexes based upon alternative weighting as described in the following case study.

MSCI, a global provider of financial indexes, data, and analytics, offers a family of fundamental factor indexes known as the MSCI Quality Indexes. MSCI weights these indexes based on a quality score used to determine a revised weighting for index constituents. The quality score is computed using a statistical process based upon standardized measures of three financial ratios for each constituent in a referenced index measuring profitability (return on equity), stability of earnings (earnings variability), and balance sheet strength (debt to equity). That is, firms with higher-than-average return on equity, less earnings variability, and a lower debt-to-equity ratio receive a higher quality score. MSCI uses the quality score to adjust the market capitalization weighting of the stock. If the score is below zero for a specific stock in the parent index, the stock will be excluded from the quality index. Alternatively, some issuers receiving sufficiently high scores will receive a higher weighting in the quality index versus the parent index. Overall, the quality indexes contain about 20% of the number of stocks in the parent index and account for about 30% of the market capitalization of the parent index.

Multi-market indexes usually comprise indexes from different groups of countries designed to represent the performance of multiple security markets. Multi-market indexes may represent multiple national markets, regions, levels of economic development, or, in some cases, the entire world. As in the case of individual shares as described in an earlier learning module, investment products based upon multi-market equity indexes provide investors the opportunity to offset a home asset bias with an index-based instrument traded on a domestic exchange. While usually denominated in the investor’s domestic currency, sources of return on these investments include gains and losses due to exchange rate changes as well as foreign equity index returns. One example for developing or emerging markets is highlighted in the following case study.

sections.title: Msci Emerging Markets Index As A Benchmark

blocks.x: The MSCI Emerging Markets Index captures large- and mid-cap issuers in representation across 24 developing markets across Asia, Africa, Europe, South America, and the Middle East. With over 1,400 constituents, the index encompasses roughly 85% of the free float-adjusted market capitalization in each jurisdiction. Asset managers create pooled investments such as mutual funds that use the periodic returns of indexes such as the MSCI Emerging Markets Index as a gauge to measure the relative performance of funds with a similar risk and return profile. For example, BlackRock’s Emerging Markets Fund (MADCX) for institutional investors uses the MSCI Emerging Markets Index to benchmark its periodic performance. The principal investment strategy of BlackRock’s fund is to invest at least 80% of its assets in countries with developing capital markets. The markets in which it invests may include, but are not limited to, those included in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index.

1. Which one of the following best describes a broad-based equity index? A. Broad-based indexes are one of the most actively traded shares on most equity exchanges. B. Broad-based indexes include the largest listed firms adjusted by market float and calculated on a market capitalization-weighted basis. C. Broad-based indexes are the benchmark for all index-based investment strategies. Solution B is correct. Broad-based indexes include the largest listed firms adjusted by market float and calculated on a market capitalization-weighted basis. Choice A is incorrect because equity indexes form the basis for products such as index-based shares but are not directly traded as shares. Choice C is incorrect as many indexes other than broad-based indexes are used as the basis for index-based investment strategies.

2. A composite index is best characterized as: A. a large-cap index. B. a multi-market index. C. a comprehensive index. Solution C is correct. A composite index generally includes securities representing more than 90% of the selected market’s value, thus making it a comprehensive index covering close to the entirety of a traded equity market. A is incorrect because a comprehensive index includes not just large-cap equities but also smaller-capitalization equities. B is incorrect because multi-market indexes are designed to represent multiple security markets but not necessarily the capitalization necessary for each market to consider them composite indexes.

3. Which one of the following most correctly describes an equity index weighted by fundamental factors? A. Weightings are never related to market capitalization. B. Weightings are based on only one fundamental factor. C. Weightings may be based on a statistical process. Solution C is correct. As in the case of the MSCI Quality Indexes, the index weightings of each stock may be calculated using a statistical process. Weightings in fundamental factor indexes are derived through statistical analysis of various company fundamentals. Their weighting is distinctly different from market capitalization-weighted indexes. A is incorrect because fundamental factor weightings may be adjusted from market capitalization by a score, as in the MSCI Quality Indexes. B is incorrect because fundamental factor weightings may be based on multiple fundamental factors, such as profitability, earnings stability, and balance sheet strength, as shown for the MSCI Quality Indexes.
TRADING

• Primary equity markets involve an issuer selling a new security or additional shares of a previously issued security to investors, while secondary markets are those in which existing shares are traded among investors.

• While exchange-based trading during regular business hours generally offers the highest liquidity, very small or very large trades are often executed off exchange via a broker (often called a block trade). Quote-driven over-the-counter trading is more common among smaller companies and usually offers less liquidity.

• Secondary equity market liquidity is measured in terms of transaction costs such as bid–offer spreads as well as other market features. A common way to assess the market liquidity of a company’s shares is to compare the proportion of shares outstanding and available to trade with the average daily number of shares traded.

• Aggregate or broad-based equity indexes allow market participants and observers to gauge the risk and return of the equity market as a whole or in part and allow for relative comparisons to the performance of individual equity securities and investor portfolios.

• Broad-based and narrower indexes, such as those based upon company size, sector, or other features, form the basis of investment products and strategies and are also used to track investment manager performance.

The following information relates to questions 1-4 Eastern States is a US public pension plan with an active allocation to publicly listed equities. Eastern States allocates some of their public equity investments to fund managers following specific strategies. With the remainder of their public equity allocation, Eastern States actively manages a portfolio of 30–50 individual stocks. The following points provide some highlights of Eastern States’ investment policy:
• As much as 10% of the total equity portfolio may be invested in allocations to IPOs.
• For stocks trading on secondary markets, a minimum of two years of public trading history is required for any new equities to be considered for purchase.
• The average daily turnover of all stock positions must meet minimum thresholds.
• Eastern States follows a globally diversified investment policy focused on large-cap stocks of companies that incorporate ESG principles.
1. Which one of the following provides the most likely argument as to why Eastern States seeks IPO allocations? A. Because of favorable long-run returns from IPOs, on average
B. Because IPOs are, on average, underpriced
C. Because IPOs are typically non-dilutive to existing shareholders

2. Which one of the following conditions may best reflect Eastern States rationale for requiring two years of trading history for secondary market purchases? A. Trading history provides the ability to assess company management quality.
B. Trading history provides the ability to forecast future company stock returns.
C. Trading history provides the ability to compare return and risk performance across similar publicly traded companies.
3. Which one of the following observable costs of trading is a likely concern for Eastern States with respect to the policy on average daily trading volume? A. Bid–ask spread costs
B. Opportunity costs
C. Market impact costs
4. Which one of the following equity index types would be most appropriate for
Eastern States to use as a benchmark for their equity portfolio performance? A. A US large-cap ESG index
B. A global ESG composite index
C. A global large-cap ESG index
Solutions

1. B is correct. IPOs, on average, experience a first-day increase in price from the price at which investors receiving an allocation in the IPO buy the shares and the closing price after the first day of public trading. Often, the level of underpricing may be 20% or greater. A is incorrect because IPO companies are often likely to underperform over long time horizons. C is incorrect because Eastern States is unlikely to be affected by the dilutive or non-dilutive effects of the IPO given that they are a new investor. As a new investor, the company is focused on the potential for underpricing benefits rather than dilution effects, unlike existing shareholders.

2. C is correct. Public market data are a critical input in comparing an individual share’s performance over time to similar firms. Furthermore, investors can easily measure returns, volatilities, and correlations across time. A is incorrect because management quality is unlikely to be assessed solely by historical stock prices but may need more examination of financial statements and other sources of company fundamental research. B is incorrect as historical stock prices do not provide information about future returns. However, they can be valuable for assessing risk and volatility.

3. A is correct. Bid–ask spreads are observable for stocks and are likely higher for stocks with relatively low daily turnover. As such, Eastern States may be looking to avoid owning stocks with high bid–ask spreads. B and C are incorrect as both opportunity and market impact costs are unobservable.

4. C is correct. Eastern States has a globally diversified portfolio of large-cap stocks in companies incorporating ESG principles. Therefore, they should benchmark with an equity index that matches those criteria. A is incorrect. Despite being a US investor, Eastern States owns a globally diversified portfolio. Thus, a US large-cap ESG index does not match the global scale. B is incorrect. The composite index includes not just large-cap stocks but also smaller stocks. Therefore, this index does not match the large-cap characteristic of Eastern States’ portfolio.

los: describe features and uses of dividends, share repurchases, stock splits, and reverse stock splits
describe dividend payment chronology
calculate price and total return for equity securities

blocks.x: The economic rights associated with equity ownership, described in earlier learning modules, drive investor returns in the form of capital appreciation and, in some cases, capital distribution. Over the long term, higher historical and expected future returns relative to other asset classes, such as bonds, make equities an attractive core holding for both individual and institutional investors. Unlike fixed-income investments, which usually have a fixed maturity and contractual cash payments, equities involve discretionary distributions over an indefinite life. In evaluating the sources of equity return, we first compare corporate actions including dividends, share buybacks, stock splits, and reverse stock splits. Next, we focus our attention on the frequency and timing of cash dividends, which are more common among mature companies. Finally, we evaluate the price and total return on equities over a holding period, which may or may not include cash dividends.

1. Which one of the following statements about regular cash dividends is most correct? A. A company is legally required to pay a regular cash dividend to shareholders if the company is profitable. B. A company with significant growth potential is likely to pay a large portion of its earnings as regular cash dividends.

C. A company’s management team and its board of directors make discretionary choices about regular cash dividend payments. Solution Choice C is correct. Regular cash dividend payments reflect discretionary decision making by a company’s management team and board as to whether regular cash dividend payments are an appropriate use of corporate cash. Choice A is incorrect because cash dividend payments to shareholders are not a legal obligation regardless of a company’s profitability. Choice B is incorrect because a company with significant growth potential is likely to reinvest more of its profits, leaving a smaller portion for potential cash dividend payments to shareholders.

2. Investors may prefer a company to repurchase shares instead of paying a cash dividend of similar size if: A. tax rates on capital gains income are lower than those on dividend income. B. repurchasing shares reduces the company’s shares outstanding. C. the company has relatively little variation in investment opportunities. Solution Choice A is correct. Investors facing higher tax rates on dividend income may prefer to receive cash distributions by selling shares and paying taxes at lower capital gains tax rates. Choice B is incorrect because a company automatically reduces shares outstanding by repurchasing shares, which should have no effect on whether investors would prefer repurchases over dividends. Choice C is incorrect because a company with little variation in investment opportunities does not require the greater flexibility associated with repurchases versus cash dividends.

3. Identify the most accurate effect of a reverse stock split on a company’s stock. A. A reverse stock split increases the number of shares outstanding. B. A reverse stock split is often used by a company that has successfully restructured its operations. C. A reverse stock split increases a company’s stock price per share. Solution Choice C is correct. A reverse stock split reduces the number of shares outstanding while increasing the stock price per share such that the market value of the company’s equity does not change. Each shareholder maintains the same proportional ownership following the reverse split. Choice A is incorrect because the number of shares outstanding increases in a stock split, not a reverse split. Choice B is incorrect because a reverse stock split is more likely with a company that is initiating a restructuring rather than with one that has just completed a successful restructuring.
4. On which one of the following dates would a company’s stock price be expected to decline, holding all else equal? A. Dividend declaration date

B. Ex-dividend date C. Dividend payment date Solution Choice B is correct. On the ex-dividend date, the stock no longer provides the owner with the right to the upcoming dividend payment. As a result, the stock price declines on this date by approximately the amount of the cash dividend, assuming no other causes for the stock to move. Choice A is incorrect because the declaration date usually precedes the ex-dividend date by a few months. Choice C is incorrect because the payment date usually follows the ex-dividend date by about two weeks.

5. Two company stocks, Vikaas and Laabhaansh, both trade at INR20 per share. Both stocks generate a 20% total return over a 1-year holding period. Vikaas pays no dividend while Laabhaansh shareholders received a dividend constituting 40% of the stock’s total return at the end of the holding period. Which one of the following is correct about the stock prices of Vikaas and Laabhaansh at the end of the holding period? A. Vikaas price is INR24.80; Laabhaansh price is INR24.00 B. Vikaas price is INR24.00; Laabhaansh price is INR22.40 C. Vikaas price is INR24.00; Laabhaansh price is INR21.60 Solution Choice B is correct. A 20% total return on a stock priced at INR20 per share implies that the numerator of the return equation is equal to INR4 per share over the holding period (= 20% × INR20). Given that Vikaas pays no dividend, this stock must increase to INR24.00 at the end of the holding period. Laabhaansh’s holding period return reflects both a dividend payment and a stock price change. Given that 40% of the total return is attributable to the dividend, 60% of the return reflects stock price appreciation. Multiplying 60% by INR4 per share equals INR2.40 per share, so Laabhaansh’s stock price is INR22.40 at the end of the holding period. Choice A is incorrect because it involves a 24% return [= (24.80 − 20)/20] on Vikaas shares and mistakenly attributes the full 20% return on Laabhaansh shares to price appreciation. Choice C is incorrect. While the Vikaas price is correct, the Laabhaansh price mistakenly multiplies the 20% expected total return by the 40% attributable to the dividend to arrive at a dividend of INR1.60 (= 8% × INR20).

6. An analyst places a two-year price target of EUR40.00 per share on a stock that is expected to pay an annual EUR1.00 per share dividend at the end of both of the next two years. The analyst believes that a 10% annual required rate of return is appropriate for the stock. Which one of the following is closest to the analyst’s estimate of today’s fair price for this stock? A. EUR34.70 B. EUR34.80 C. EUR34.90 Solution Choice B is correct. The analyst solves for the price by incorporating the expected dividend cash flow of EUR1.00 at the end of each of the next two
years with the target price of EUR40.00 at the end of two years with the following equation:
Today's price = _ 1.10 + _

. 1.10 The solution equals EUR34.79 per share. Choice A is incorrect because it assumes that both annual dividends are received at the end of two years. Choice C is incorrect because it fails to incorporate the present value of the dividend received in one year.
SPLITS
describe features and uses of dividends, share repurchases, stock splits, and reverse stock splits

As owners of the company, shareholders are entitled to any discretionary capital distributions made by the company on a proportional basis. These distributions are referred to as dividends and vary in terms of timing and type. For example, while many corporate issuers regularly distribute cash to investors, others may make a one-time distribution or pay no dividends at all. These distributions are typically authorized by a firm’s board of directors and may be subject to consent by a shareholder vote in some jurisdictions.

Cash Dividends Cash distributions paid at known intervals are referred to as regular cash dividends. These distributions represent a cash return of capital to shareholders. Companies in an early stage of their life cycle with significant growth potential are more likely to reinvest cash flows and as a result less likely to distribute cash to shareholders. As companies mature and generate higher cash flows, they may have fewer growth opportunities, so they are more likely to initiate and pay cash dividends. However, each company’s management team and board must assess whether to distribute a portion of company earnings as dividends. In some cases, highly profitable companies choose to pay no dividends. Those firms that pay cash dividends usually do so with consistent frequency (e.g., quarterly in the United States and Canada; usually semiannually in Europe and Japan; and usually annually in Scandinavia, China, and elsewhere). Many companies attempt to maintain a relatively consistent and constant dividend per share, seeking to avoid dividend changes that investors may interpret as an improvement or deterioration in the issuer’s future earnings prospects. Dividend payments have a signal and informational value; maintaining consistent dividends signals management confidence that a cash distribution does not meaningfully reduce a company’s future growth and profitability. Alternatively, expected weaker company performance or improved growth prospects may lead management to reduce or eliminate dividends to preserve cash.

Similarly, companies often forego a dividend increase if a rise in earnings or cash flow generation is unlikely to be sustained. In cases where a company experiences significant restructuring, strategic disruption, or earnings changes over the economic cycle, cash dividends may be forced to fluctuate, as described in the next example.
Example 1

Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV Dividend Changes Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV (ABI), the world’s largest brewer, was formed by combining Brazilian beverages company AmBev, the Belgian-based drinks firm InBev, and Anheuser Busch, the largest US brewing company. Over the 15 years following the acquisition of Anheuser-Busch in 2008, ABI’s fortunes fluctuated as reflected in both its earnings per share (EPS) and dividends per share (DPS), as shown in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1: Anheuser-Busch InBev EPS and DPS, 2009 to 2022

Source: Bloomberg. The early years of the ABI merger were met with investor enthusiasm. During the seven years following the Anheuser-Busch acquisition, ABI’s stock price grew by nearly 10 times from a low of EUR12.89 at the end of November 2008 to a high of EUR121.95 at the end of November 2015, with its dividend rising from less than EUR1 to over EUR6.00 per share. In late 2015, ABI announced its acquisition of SABMiller, its primary rival in the global beer market, a deal that was finalized in October 2016 at a price of over USD100 billion. Unfortunately, the acquisition coincided with a slowdown in beer demand and subsequent production decline. Due to ABI’s dominant position as a newly merged company in multiple parts of the world, regulatory approval of the SABMiller deal required ABI to sell key brands in several countries under less favorable market conditions. Earnings suffered as a result, leading ABI to cut its dividend in each of the years 2018, 2019, and 2020, reaching a low of EUR0.50 per share. It wasn’t until 2023 that ABI was able to once again increase dividends given its slow post-COVID earnings recovery.

While tax policies vary by jurisdiction, investors are typically subject to income tax on cash dividends in the tax period they are received. In some jurisdictions, corporations are legally required to withhold taxes on gross dividends and only distribute net dividends.

An extraordinary or special cash dividend is paid by a company that either does not pay dividends on a regular schedule or pays as a one-time cash payment that supplements a regular dividend. Companies may use special dividends to reward shareholders with a one-time distribution of unexpectedly high earnings or pay out cash proceeds from the liquidation of an investment, as described in the following example.

Ford Motor Company, a US-based multinational manufacturer of commercial and passenger vehicles, missed earnings expectations in 4Q and full year 2022 due to several factors, including “execution issues” and limited profitability of its electric vehicle segment. Despite reporting a net loss in 2022, Ford announced a special dividend in February 2023 of USD0.65 per share. The dividend involved a distribution related to Ford’s sale of around 90% of its ownership stake in Rivian, a new electric vehicle company in which it held a strategic equity stake. This sale of more than 90 million shares over the course of 2022 resulted in a gain to Ford of USD1.8 billion. Shareholders received the supplemental dividend of USD0.65 per share in addition to Ford’s regular cash dividend of USD0.15 per share.

As in the above example, special dividends are typically larger than those regularly paid to shareholders. Another form of extraordinary dividend is a liquidating dividend, which involves a return of capital rather than an earnings distribution. Liquidating dividends are used when a company ceases operations and distributes its net assets or sells a portion of its business for cash and distributes the proceeds. The use of a liquidating dividend may also involve a distribution that exceeds a firm’s accumulated retained earnings.

Share Repurchases Share repurchases provide an alternative way to distribute cash in contrast to cash dividend payments. A share repurchase (or buyback) is a transaction in which a company uses available cash to buy back its own shares. In contrast to cash receipts from dividend payments that are received by all shareholders of a company, cash receipts from share repurchases are only received by shareholders who voluntarily choose to sell. Shares that have been repurchased are not considered for dividends, voting, or computing earnings per share. A share repurchase is viewed as equivalent to the payment of cash dividends of equal value in terms of the effect on total shareholder wealth, although differences in realized returns among shareholders occur, as illustrated in the following example.

The two mechanisms for distributing cash in the example have a similar aggregate effect, although the impact on individual shareholders may differ. Company managers cite several reasons for engaging in share repurchases:
• Signals a view that shares are undervalued, or, more generally, to support share prices and/or change an issuer’s debt-to-equity ratio

• Offers an issuer greater flexibility in the amount and timing of cash distribution to shareholders versus regular cash dividends because of the ability to reduce cash payouts when the issuer has relatively more investment opportunities

• Offers investors greater flexibility in managing investment returns, providing tax efficiency in markets where tax rates on dividends paid to investors exceed tax rates on capital gains, and avoids double taxation
• Enables firms to manage the number of outstanding shares due to the exercise of employee stock options to manage the impact on earnings per share

• Enables firms to increase earnings per share by reducing shares outstanding during a reporting period While many dividend-paying companies make efforts to maintain consistency in their distribution of regular cash dividends, stock repurchases may be announced in advance on a multi-year basis but conducted opportunistically based on market conditions, as described next.

sections.title: Adidas Ag Dividend And Stock Repurchase History

blocks.x: Adidas, the German athletic footwear and clothing marketer, historically limited its shareholder distributions to dividends. Starting in 2014, the company announced a EUR1.5 billion, three-year share buyback program. The first repurchase tranche of EUR300 million was executed in November 2014 at an average of EUR61, or well below Adidas’ EUR75 average share price for the first nine months of the year. However, cash distributions through buybacks remained consistently below cash distributions through dividend payments to shareholders.

In March 2018, Adidas announced a new three-year plan to repurchase EUR3 billion of its stock. From 2018 to 2020, Adidas spent nearly double the cash on share repurchases that it paid in dividends, marking a major shift in its shareholder distribution strategy. The company continued its buyback plans with over EUR1 billion in 2021 and over EUR2.5 billion in 2022, which included proceeds from its divestiture of Reebok. In 2021, management announced a plan to continue to distribute most of its free cash flow to shareholders, with 30% to 50% of net income in the form of dividends and expected buybacks of over EUR8 billion through 2025.

Some companies choose to distribute returns to shareholders entirely through stock repurchases. For example, many large US technology firms, such as Alphabet, have never paid dividends but consistently spend billions of dollars each quarter to buy back stock.

Stock Dividends, Stock Splits, and Reverse Splits A stock dividend (or bonus issue of shares) is a type of dividend in which a company distributes newly issued shares instead of cash to shareholders. In some cases, this may involve the distribution of the company’s existing common shares, while in others, a company may spin off an existing division as a new company. For example, when the US conglomerate General Electric embarked on a plan to shed businesses and narrow its strategic focus to the aerospace industry, it distributed common shares of new stand-alone companies from existing divisions, including health care (GE HealthCare Technologies) and electric power generation (GE Vernova Inc.), to shareholders. In contrast to a cash dividend, a stock dividend of a company’s own shares divides the firm’s market value of shareholders’ equity into smaller pieces without a change in the value or any shareholder’s proportional ownership in the company. Thus, stock dividends are neither a source of income nor relevant for valuation purposes. Specific forms of stock dividends include stock splits and reverse stock splits. A stock split, sometimes referred to as a forward split, involves an increase in the number of shares outstanding and a proportionate decrease in the price per share such that the total market value of equity as well as investors’ proportional ownership claim in the company are unchanged. A common reason for issuers to consider a stock split includes maintaining a unit price per share within an optimal range for trading purposes. A very low or high unit price per share can affect trading dynamics via a stock’s bid–offer spread. For example, a trader showing a bid–ask spread of USD0.03 per share for a company stock trading at USD4.00 may discourage investors due to the relatively high 1.5% cost (= 0.03 × 2 ÷ 4) to acquire and subsequently sell shares. The same USD0.03 spread for a USD1,000 share price results in just a 0.006% (= 0.03 × 2 ÷ 1,000) charge, which may not be sufficient to attract market makers to provide liquidity. Equity issuer approaches to stock splits vary widely, as described in the following example.

sections.title: Stock Split Policies Of Amazon.Com Versus Berkshire Hathaway

blocks.x: Two major US corporations, Amazon.com and Berkshire Hathaway, offer an interesting contrast in stock split behavior. Amazon.com went public as an online book retailer in June 1997, and the company’s share price rose to approximately 50 times the initial public offering (IPO) price during the internet boom of the late 1990s. Amazon.com shares split three separate times over this period, with an original share equivalent to 12 shares by September 1999. At the beginning

of 2000, Amazon’s price per share was near USD80 per share, and by the end of 2021, each share traded at well over USD3,000. In 2022, as stock prices declined, Amazon.com split its stock 20:1, lowering the price per share to closer to USD100. Berkshire Hathaway has taken a very different approach to its rising share price. The company’s Class A shares went public in March 1980 at USD290 per share. By the end of 2022, each Class A share of Berkshire Hathaway traded at around USD542,000 per share, a 186,900% price increase with no splits during the life of the Class A shares. However, relenting to pressure from shareholders seeking to directly own individual shares at a lower price, Berkshire Hathaway issued Class B shares in 1996 at 1/30 of the price of Class A shares. In 2010, the Class B shares split on a 50:1 basis and now trade at approximately 1/1,500 of the Class A share price.

A reverse stock split involves a decrease in the number of shares outstanding and a proportionate increase in the price per share such that the total market value of equity and investors’ proportional ownership claim in the company do not change. Common reasons for issuers to consider a reverse stock split include maintaining a minimum price per share to meet exchange requirements as well as bringing the current price into a range more optimal for trading purposes at a time when a firm takes measures to turn around or restructure its business.

In 1942, Joseph-Armand Bombardier founded a company bearing his name to build and sell his snowmobile invention. In the following decades, Bombardier went public and expanded globally as a manufacturer of recreational equipment, rail transport equipment, and commercial aircraft. After narrowly averting bankruptcy, the company initiated a multiyear plan to shed most of its divisions, pay down debt, and focus solely on corporate jet production. Bombardier’s share price declined by almost 95% from a peak in July 2018 to a low of CAD0.28 in November 2020. While the price recovered to well over CAD1.00 per share in 2021, early the following year, Bombardier shareholders voted to consolidate both Class A shares (with multiple votes) and Class B (single vote shares) on a 25-for-1 basis as of June 2022. The reverse split reduced the number of shares outstanding by a factor of 25 while increasing Bombardier’s price per share to CAD26.86 on the split date. Despite an initial negative market reaction, market sentiment improved as the company successfully executed its focused strategy, with the price per share exceeding CAD50 by the end of 2023.

1. Investors in Kettlewood Corporation have received cash dividends per share of GBP10 for the past three years. Kettlewood decides to halve its dividend and use the remaining cash to repurchase shares. Which one of the following statements best describes the impact of this change on the realized returns of Kettlewood’s shareholders? A. All Kettlewood shareholders will experience a 50% reduction in their realized return after the change. B. Since Kettlewood distributes the same amount of cash as in the past, all Kettlewood shareholders will have the same realized return after the change.

C. All Kettlewood shareholders will experience a 50% reduction in their realized return, except for those who choose to sell their shares. Solution Choice C is correct. All shareholders will experience a halving of the cash dividend, with only those who choose to sell receiving additional cash and any realized earnings. Choice A is incorrect because it excludes those shareholders who choose to sell their shares back to the company for cash. Choice B is incorrect because not all shareholders will choose to sell shares back to the company in exchange for cash, and only those who do will realize the return.

2. A share repurchase differs from cash dividend payments because: A. repurchases decrease shareholder proportional ownership stakes while dividends do not. B. repurchases are not direct cash distributions to shareholders, unlike cash dividends. C. repurchases may provide signals to the market about an issuer’s perception of share value, while dividends do not. Solution Choice C is correct. When an issuer repurchases its stock, investors may consider this to be a signal that management believes its stock is undervalued. Cash dividends provide no signal about the stock’s value (although an increase may signal management’s expectation of higher future earnings, and this signal requires more than simply the payment of dividends). Choice A is incorrect because the repurchase increases the proportional ownership of all shareholders who do not participate in the stock repurchase. Only shareholders who choose to sell might reduce their proportional ownership. Choice B is incorrect because repurchases are a cash distribution to shareholders. The difference is that only selling shareholders receive the distribution from repurchases.

3. Baixo Corporation’s stock recently increased from EUR800 to EUR1,600 per share. Baixo’s chief financial officer decides to split the company’s stock to achieve a price between EUR70 and EUR90 per share. Which one of the following is the most appropriate split adjustment for Baixo? A. 10:1 B. 20:1 C. 25:1 Solution Choice B is correct. At a price of EUR1,600 per share, a 20:1 split would decrease Baixo’s price per share to approximately EUR80 per share. The payout of regular cash dividends to common shareholders generally follows a standard timeline, as shown in the hypothetical example in Exhibit 2.

While timing varies, the dividend payout process is set into motion once the company’s board of directors (and shareholders, as necessary) votes to pay the dividend.
• First is the declaration date, the day that the company issues a statement declaring a specific dividend.

• This is followed by the ex-dividend date (or ex-date), the first date that a share trades without (or “ex”) the dividend. The ex-dividend date is followed closely (one or two business days later) by the record date, or the date that a shareholder registered with a securities depositary is deemed to own the shares for purposes of receiving the upcoming dividend.

• The difference between the ex-dividend date and the record date is linked to equity market trade settlement. Settlement refers to the official transfer of securities to the buyer’s account and cash to the seller’s account. If an equity trade settlement takes two days, usually there is a two-day gap between the ex-dividend date and the record date, ensuring all transactions made before the ex-dividend date are settled by the record date.

• The final step in the process is the payment date, which is the day that the company electronically transfers a dividend payment to shareholders. Exhibit 3 shows the impact of a USD1.00 per share dividend from the prior day’s closing price to the closing price on the ex-dividend date.

As buyers of a company’s shares on or after the ex-dividend date are ineligible to receive the pending dividend, all else being equal, the company’s share price immediately falls by the amount of the foregone dividend on that day. 1. Wiley Creek Limited declared a quarterly dividend of AUD1.25 per share on its common stock on Monday, 7 January. The dividend was payable on 1 February to shareholders of record on 10 January. On which one of the following business days would a decline in Wiley Creek’s stock price of the dividend amount, holding all else equal, be expected? A. 9 January B. 10 January C. 1 February Solution Choice A is correct. The ex-dividend date is the first date at which the stock trades without rights to the upcoming dividend payment. The ex-dividend date typically occurs one business day before the record date. In this case, 10 January is the record date, so 9 January is the most likely ex-dividend date. Choice B is incorrect because the record date occurs after the ex-dividend date. Choice C is incorrect because the payment date occurs several weeks later than the ex-dividend date.

2. A junior analyst proposes the following short-term trading strategy: Buy stocks on the date before their ex-dividend dates, and then sell the stocks following the dividend payment date. Which one of the following statements is most correct about this trading strategy? A. This trading strategy will likely be profitable, on average, because of returns from collecting dividends.

B. This trading strategy will likely generate negative profits, on average, because of the combined effect of market movements and company-specific price changes. C. This trading strategy will likely earn profits, on average, proportional to market movements. Solution Choice C is correct. Buying before the ex-dividend date and selling after collecting the dividend, on average, should generate zero profits because the stock price should decline by the amount of the dividend. The effect of company-specific price changes should be canceled by trading in many different stocks. The only profits (positive or negative) will be based on market movements between the purchase and sale dates for each stock. Choice A is incorrect because the dividends collected simply offset the price declines on the ex-dividend dates. Choice B is incorrect because profits could be positive or negative, depending on market movements. Company-specific price changes should be eliminated because of the diversified trading strategy.

RETURNS

• Regular cash dividends are a source of periodic income and subject to tax. While share repurchases have a similar wealth effect for owners, they also support share prices and offer flexibility and tax efficiency to some investors.

• Stock splits and reverse splits change the number of shares outstanding, with a proportional change in share price, but do not affect shareholder wealth, a firm’s equity market value, or an investor’s ownership claim.

• Once a cash dividend is declared, a date is specified upon which shares are traded without receiving the future dividend, at which time the share price typically drops by the amount of the future dividend.
• Shareholders entitled to receive dividends are typically identified on a date before a dividend payment is made. Dividend payments are made based upon the number of shares held as of that date.
• Sources of equity holding period return include any cash distributions and share appreciation or depreciation over the time horizon.
• A stock’s price should equal the present value of expected future cash distributions and the expected future sale price at the end of a holding period.

blocks.x: VALUATION | 1

Earlier Equities learning modules addressed the economic and voting rights of shareholders as well as equity issuance, trading, and sources of return. We now turn our attention to how investors and financial analysts assess the value of equity securities. If equity markets are informationally efficient, then the current observed market price per share should reflect all available information and the aggregated views of market participants. Investors can attempt to evaluate the intrinsic value of a stock using different approaches. These approaches are meant to generate indicators or estimates of a stock’s true intrinsic value. We refer to these estimates generated by investors as perceived value indicators of the stock. As investors may use different approaches and information, with varying levels of risk tolerance and investment time horizons, these perceived values may differ, sometimes greatly, across investors. Differences between investor perceived value and current market price are a key driver of issuer and investor decisions. Equity valuation typically involves a financial analyst’s assessment of whether today’s market price for a share accurately reflects the present value of expected future cash flows over a specific period. These assessment methods rely on information about the company at a point in time. As new information about the company and its prospects becomes available, an analyst’s assessment and even the true intrinsic share value may change.

In this learning module, we first contrast price and value, assessing market-based and accounting-based measures often used in the equity valuation process. We then introduce equity valuation approaches that assess company performance on an absolute or relative basis and their advantages and disadvantages. The details of valuation models applying these approaches are the subject of subsequent learning modules.

1. Which one of the following statements is most correct about price and value of an equity security? A. Equity market price must reflect its intrinsic value. B. Equity market price is observed while its intrinsic value is unobserved. C. Equity market price reflects investor agreement on the security’s expected value. Solution: B is correct. Choice B is correct because a firm’s equity market price is observed, while intrinsic value reflects the collective (and differing) expectations of market participants. Each market participant has their own unobserved value of an equity security. Choice A is incorrect because this statement implies that a stock is always fairly valued, which does not allow for periods of overvaluation or undervaluation. Choice C is incorrect because a stock’s price reflects differing expectations of a stock’s value among investors.

2. An analyst estimates the intrinsic value of a stock to be in the range of EUR17.85 to EUR21.45. Recent stock trading has been in a market price range from EUR21.15 to EUR24.35. Assuming the analyst’s intrinsic value range for the stock is accurate, this stock is most likely: A. overvalued. B. undervalued. C. fairly valued. Solution: A is correct. Choice A is correct because the range of intrinsic values is almost entirely below the range of recent trading prices. Thus, the price is likely greater than value. Choice B is incorrect because the range of intrinsic values needs to be greater than the range of traded prices for the stock to likely be undervalued. Choice C is incorrect because the overlap in the two ranges is very small from EUR21.15 to EUR21.45. Almost all of the price range lies above the intrinsic value range.
3. Which one of the following assets is most likely to be deducted in an analyst’s adjustment of book value of equity? A. Short-term investments B. Inventories

C. Goodwill Solution: C is correct. Choice C is correct because goodwill is an intangible asset and financial analysts typically exclude intangible assets when calculating the book value of equity. Choice A is incorrect because short-term investments are part of a company’s tangible assets and thus included in book value calculations. Choice B is incorrect because inventories are part of a company’s tangible assets and thus included in book value calculations.

4. The market value of equity for a company can be calculated as enterprise value: A. minus market value of debt, preferred stock, and cash and short-term investments. B. plus market value of debt and preferred stock minus cash and shortterm investments. C. minus market value of debt and preferred stock plus cash and shortterm investments. Solution: C is correct. Choice C is correct because enterprise value is calculated as the market value of equity plus the market value of debt and preferred stock minus cash and short-term investments. Therefore, the market value of equity is enterprise value minus the market value of debt and preferred stock plus cash and short-term investments. Choice A is incorrect because this description states that cash and shortterm investments are subtracted instead of added. Choice B is incorrect because this description reverses the correct arithmetic operations on both debt plus preferred stock and cash and short-term investments.

5. Which of the following is most likely considered a weakness of present value models? A. Present value models cannot be used for companies that do not pay dividends. B. Changes in model assumptions and inputs can result in large changes in the computed intrinsic value of the security. C. The value of the security depends on the investor’s holding period; thus, comparing valuations of different companies for different investors is difficult. Solution: B is correct. Choice B is correct because computed values can be sensitive to changes in inputs, such as required rate of return or growth rates. Choice A is incorrect because other present value models, such as free cash flow to equity (FCFE) or residual income models, can be used to value companies that do not pay dividends. Choice C is incorrect because the intrinsic value computed from a present value model should be independent of the investor’s holding period.

6. An analyst is attempting to calculate the intrinsic value of a company and has gathered the following data for similar companies as well as the company being valued: EBITDA, total market value, and market value of cash and short-term investments, debt, and preferred shares. The analyst is most likely to use: A. a multiplier model. B. a present value model. C. an asset-based valuation model. Solution: A is correct. Choice A is correct because the analyst has gathered sufficient information to calculate the enterprise value to EBITDA multiple for comparable firms and to compare this multiple to that of the company of interest. Choice B is incorrect because the analyst requires dividend, FCFE or FCFF (free cash flow to the firm), growth rate expectations, and a required return estimate to use a present value model. Choice C is incorrect because the analyst requires market value estimates of the company’s specific assets and liabilities individually.
contrast price and value for an equity security

Market Price, Intrinsic Value, and Investor Perceived Value While sometimes used interchangeably, the price and value of a security can have very different meanings for financial analysts who work with issuers or investors. The observed market price of a firm’s equity at which it may be freely bought and sold in the secondary market reflects the collective (and differing) expectations of market participants regarding the amount, timing, and uncertainty of the firm’s future cash flows available to its owners. The intrinsic value of a firm’s share is generally an unobserved and unobservable quantity. Intrinsic value (or fundamental value) is based on key characteristics that affect a firm’s future cash flows. Financial analysts often view a firm’s intrinsic value as based on the “true” present value of a share’s expected future cash flows using an appropriate discount rate. While this approach to intrinsic value is common for firms whose equity is traded in primary or secondary markets, cases exist in which a firm’s intrinsic value and future cash flows depend greatly on the transaction and the parties involved. For example, in a merger, a firm’s intrinsic value relies heavily on how well the acquired firm may be integrated into the acquiring firm to generate additional value. For this learning module, we focus on the true present value of a share’s discounted expected future cash flows when considering intrinsic value. While an equity security has only one market price at any given time, each market participant has their own perceived value of the equity security. These individual assessments of how a security should be priced may vary widely and differ significantly

from the observed market price. These differences can influence both investor decisions, such as the purchase or sale of shares, as well as issuer decisions, including the issuance of new shares or repurchase of outstanding stock. These decisions are predicated on the assumption that as market participants digest new information and take actions to capitalize on differences between current market prices and perceived value, these forces will cause the share price to converge over time to its true intrinsic value.

Investor Approaches to Determining Perceived Value Market participants use three major approaches to develop perceived values that they use as guides to a firm’s intrinsic value: 1. Naive or story-based valuation 2. Relative valuation 3. Absolute or fundamental valuation Each approach is described briefly below, and the latter two are addressed later in more detail in this and later learning modules. The first approach is naive or story-based valuation. A naive valuation approach focuses on a narrative about a company’s value that is not directly linked to an in-depth economic or financial evaluation. This approach is often used for companies known as meme stocks or cult companies. Meme stocks are company shares for which investors make investment decisions heavily influenced by social media posts, while cult companies are those for which investor decisions may be based upon a loyal or fanatical product following rather than expected company performance. Naive valuation may also feature in market “bubbles” to justify an excessively high or low valuation of a company, a sector, or even an entire market. While a naive evaluation may prove correct in the end, it is not based on any type of deep analysis of the share value. Relative valuation uses observed financial or market information to develop indicators of value that are compared to a relevant peer group. A company or sector is then said to be over- or undervalued relative to the indicators of the chosen peer group. An example of a relative value indicator is the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) or price-to-book ratio (P/B). The chosen indicators for a company and its peer group must be appropriate and calculated consistently to serve as a useful estimate of intrinsic value. Absolute or fundamental valuation is an approach to estimating share prices using expected cash flows introduced in the prior learning module. For example, recall that we calculated the present value of expected dividends per share plus the future expected share price at the end of n periods with an annualized equity discount rate of re. Using actual cash distributions to shareholders is one approach, while others include assessing expected cash flows available to investors as well as relative comparisons to other equity issuers or equity rate of return-based estimates. In each case, we seek to establish an intrinsic value (IVt) assessment at time t. We may show this using the example of a generalized discounted cash flow approach as in Equation 1:

where the expected share price in n periods is denoted E(Pt+n) and the expected periodic cash flow available to investors is E(CFt+i). This assessment requires us to estimate the expected future price using today’s information. As we will see in later lessons, an important value distinction involves whether the intrinsic value of the firm is measured from an enterprise value perspective, that is, from the point of view of both debtholders and shareholders, or the assessment focuses solely on equityholders based on share price.

A well-constructed equity valuation model seeks to estimate share value while eliminating the individual biases incorporated by market participants. The result of such an unbiased model is an estimate of intrinsic value (or fundamental value) that is distinct from the current market share price. Intrinsic value is based on analyzing key characteristics believed to be essential elements affecting a firm’s future cash flows. An analyst estimating the intrinsic value of an equity security often uses more than one valuation approach to arrive at a value estimate. The rise during the COVID-19 pandemic of meme stocks is an extreme example of the divergence between a share’s market price and value, as described in the following case study.

The Meteoric Rise and Fall of GameStop Corporation’s (GME) Share Price Based in the United States, GameStop is the world’s largest video game retailer with over 4,400 stores in North America, Europe, and Australia. The rise in online shopping caused the company’s fortunes to decline as it closed stores and ceased dividend payments in 2019, a trend that accelerated during the initial months of the COVID-19 pandemic. Institutional investors who believed that the GME share price continued to exceed its intrinsic value borrowed and sold shares short to gain from continued price declines. In mid-2020, the aggregate short position in GME shares was equivalent to over 25 times the average daily trading volume, making it one of the most widely shorted US stocks during that time.

Individual investors viewing social media sites such as the WallStreetBets Reddit forum were swayed by a narrative that GME would survive as a company and that share purchases would punish professional short sellers. To force short sellers to cover losses, retail investors aggressively purchased GME shares, driving up trading volumes and prices sharply in early 2021, as shown in Exhibit 1. GameStop’s shares jumped from a low of under USD1 in mid-2020 to nearly USD87 at its peak in early 2021, adjusting for the effects of a 4-for-1 stock split in July 2022. The company’s management took advantage of its elevated share price to issue new shares twice in the first half of 2021. The company initially sold 3.5 million shares for gross proceeds of over USD550 million and used

almost half of the proceeds to retire all its long-term debt. It then raised an additional USD1.13 billion by selling 20 million new shares at a price of roughly USD56 in June of 2021 to invest in new growth initiatives.

Investor Perceived Value, Market Prices, and Market Dynamics The example of GameStop highlights how the actions of both investors and issuers often interact. Differences in perceived value of a company’s shares across investor types, such as institutional and individual investors, as well as company management can generate price dynamics as the market seeks to find a market-clearing share price that reflects these conflicting valuations. For example, when considering a firm’s intrinsic value from the perspective of shareholders, comparison of the market share price Pt to the estimated value IVt leads a financial analyst to one of the following conclusions: Share is currently undervalued: Pt < IVt Share is currently overvalued: Pt > IVt Share is fairly valued: Pt ≈ IVt Investors will either increase (for an undervalued security) or decrease share exposure to earn a portfolio return greater than re under the assumption that the market price-to-value difference will narrow over the holding period. Issuers, on the other hand, often view undervaluation as a share repurchase opportunity and overvaluation as leading to additional share issuance. In the GameStop example, institutional investors considered the market price for the company’s shares to be overvalued, presumably based on a relative or absolute valuation analysis. This perception led the institutional investors to reduce GME exposure and even take a short position in GME shares. In contrast, individual investors swayed by social media posts considered GME to be undervalued. Their purchases pushed market prices higher, contrary to what institutional investors expected. This push led to short-run losses for investors who evaluated GameStop based on relative or absolute valuation analyses. Finally, GameStop’s management, seeing the sharp rise in their share price, acted to raise capital through share issuance. This action allowed management to raise far more capital than at a lower market price, providing GME with an unexpected source of funding to address its business challenges. This example demonstrates the complex market dynamics associated with differences in perceived values across investors and even the issuer itself. Exhibit 2 provides a high-level summary of how actions of both investors and issuers depend on their perceived values versus the market price.

While market prices are readily observable, true intrinsic value may be more difficult to ascertain with a high degree of certainty. For example, stocks of issuers with stable, predictable growth that commonly distribute regular cash dividends are more

straightforward to value than those experiencing rapid growth, cyclicality, or substantial change. Valuation estimates are more likely to diverge across market participants for “harder to value” stocks. The level of conviction surrounding value estimates combined with their divergence from market prices influences whether market participants act based on the results of an equity valuation exercise.

An investor analyzes a stock and concludes that it is currently undervalued. The investor values the stock at EUR26.59 and buys shares at the current market price of EUR21.65. The stock is not expected to pay any cash dividends.

2. Identify two reasons why the investor may not achieve a positive result from buying this stock during the holding period. Solution:

1. The investor’s valuation model incorrectly interpreted information about the stock or incorporated individual biases that caused the valuation to be higher than it should have been. 2. Negative information about the company’s expected future performance emerged during the investor’s holding period.

Market changes and additional information affect both share prices and valuation drivers, leading analysts to typically consider ranges rather than point estimates for both Pt and IVt. In the case of share prices, analysts frequently reference a share’s price range as defined by its recent high and low price. A value estimate range may apply to more than one valuation method and/or change the key model inputs used under a single valuation method based on scenario analysis. Scenario analysis combines a base case valuation with alternative outcomes, allowing the use of more favorable (bullish) or adverse (bearish) forecasts in the valuation process: n

where Pt,i is the expected share price at time t under scenario i. There are various approaches available for estimating a security’s intrinsic value, and within each approach there are often multiple different ways to estimate value. It is important for an analyst to be able to compare these various estimates against one another and against recent experience with the security’s market price. This synthesis-of-valuation approach seeks to identify ranges for intrinsic value produced by a variety of approaches and compare that to the range of the stock’s price over the recent past. The prior knowledge check illustrates that an analyst often assigns probabilities to different equity valuation scenarios based upon judgment. The building blocks used to estimate firm value as well as the most common valuation approaches are the subject of the following lessons.

1. Which one of the following statements provides the most correct characterization of meme stocks? A. Meme stocks typically exhibit low trading volumes and high volatility. B. Meme stocks can show extreme divergence between price and value. C. Meme stocks typically are undervalued. Solution: B is correct. Choice B is correct because high trading volumes from strong individual investor buying behavior cause price to temporarily diverge from intrinsic value. Choice A is incorrect because meme stocks typically exhibit high, not low, trading volumes. Choice C is incorrect because prices of meme stocks typically increase above intrinsic value and thus are likely to be overvalued.

2. A corporate issuer’s chief financial officer values its shares between USD50 and USD60; these shares have recently traded at prices between USD44 and USD51. Which one of the following most correctly describes an appropriate action by this corporate issuer? A. The issuer should issue new shares of company stock. B. The issuer should repurchase shares of company stock. C. The issuer should neither issue shares nor repurchase shares of company stock. Solution: B is correct. Choice B is correct because the company’s chief financial officer believes the stock to be undervalued. Repurchasing undervalued shares is an appropriate action for a corporate issuer. Choice A is incorrect because an issuer is more likely to issue new shares when they are overvalued, not undervalued. Choice C is incorrect because this statement more accurately describes the appropriate action if the company’s shares are fairly valued.

3. Which one of the following is most likely to be true for a stock that is easier to value compared to a stock that is harder to value? A. Less divergence between price and intrinsic value B. Higher potential future rates of return

C. More cyclicality in profits and dividends Solution: A is correct. Choice A is correct because valuation estimates are more likely to diverge across market participants for harder-to-value stocks. Choice B is incorrect because the greater divergence for harder-to-value stocks increases the potential for high returns, although this divergence also increases the potential for negative returns on these stocks. Choice C is incorrect because stocks of companies with more cyclicality may be harder to value.
contrast the use of book value of equity, market capitalization, and enterprise value as indicators of intrinsic value

In establishing a firm’s estimated value using an equity valuation approach, financial analysts often employ observable measures based upon financial statements or market data to gain further insight into the intrinsic value of an equity security, namely the book value of equity, market capitalization, and enterprise value.

Book Value of Equity The book value of equity (BVEt) represents the difference between the carrying value of assets and liabilities in a firm’s audited financial statements: BVEt = Book value (Assets)t− Book value (Liabilities)t.	            (3)

Shareholder’s equity includes closely held shares but excludes minority interest as it represents a non-controlling stake with limited control over ownership decisions. As illustrated in Exhibit 4, the measurement of a firm’s net assets is based on balance sheet items. As discussed in earlier Financial Statement Analysis learning modules, balance sheet items may reflect historical cost or market values. Furthermore, depreciation and amortization methods affect the reported balance sheet amounts of fixed assets. In the case of tangible assets, differences in historical cost and depreciation methods can distort book value comparisons across firms. For example, newer fixed assets are less depreciated and therefore reflected in financial statements at a higher carrying value than older assets. Intangible assets—or non-monetary, non-physical items of value owned or controlled by a company and that provide economic benefits—may not be consistently recorded in accounting statements. For example, the treatment of intellectual property, such as patents, licenses, or trademarks, differs depending upon whether they are internally generated or purchased from a third party. If identifiable, intangible assets generated internally are usually expensed in a single period. In contrast, intangible assets that are purchased are amortized over multiple periods if their useful life is finite or subject to impairment tests if they are of use for an indefinite period. Balance sheet assets also include any portion of the purchase price of companies acquired that exceeds the fair value of identifiable assets and liabilities, referred to as goodwill. For these reasons, the assets of acquisitive companies may overstate a firm’s underlying capacity to generate future cash flow versus firms with organic growth. As a result, financial analysts typically exclude intangible assets when calculating book value. Book value has greater relevance as a value measure for firms with significant tangible assets and similar asset structures and is less useful for asset-light companies or early-stage firms where the balance sheet may not reflect future earnings potential. A firm’s book value of equity reflects the past historical operating and financing decisions of its management as well as abrupt changes, such as the write-down of assets highlighted in the following case study.
ØRSTED A/S ASSET WRITE-DOWNS

Ørsted A/S, a Danish company, operates in the renewable energy sector and is one of the world’s largest offshore wind farm developers. One of Ørsted’s largest projects was a 2.2 GW (gigawatt) offshore wind farm to be located off the coast of New Jersey. While the project’s initial phase received US government approval for construction in July 2023, the company canceled the project in October 2023 due to supplier delays, tax credit limitations, and unforeseen cost increases. The project cancellation resulted in Ørsted reporting over DKK19 billion in asset write-downs in its 2023 income statement and contributed to a decline in the company’s book value of equity from DKK95.5 billion at year-end 2022 to DKK77.8 billion at year-end 2023. Ørsted’s stock price initially declined almost 25% on 30 August as the company first announced the pending write-downs of wind farm assets, and its market capitalization fell over 40% between the second and third quarters of 2023.

The book value of liabilities typically includes long-term debt and other liabilities carried at face value but may also underestimate any contingent liabilities arising from sources such as product liability, environmental, or legal risks not fully captured on a firm’s balance sheet in accounting terms.

Aside from the difference between assets and liabilities, the book value of equity may be separately calculated as the sum of shareholder’s equity line items in a company’s audited financial statements shown as follows: Shareholder's equity = Shares capital + Additional paid-in capital

+ Retained earnings − Treasury stock.	                                     (5) When an issuer has a negative book value of equity, it may signal a greater risk of financial distress or bankruptcy given a company’s hypothetical inability to meet outstanding obligations with existing assets based upon accounting measures. That said, firms experiencing rapid growth or asset impairment may continue to add value for investors despite a negative book value of equity. In other cases, a company’s distribution policy choices, such as share repurchases, combined with the distortions associated with measurement of intangible assets may contribute to sustained negative equity for well-performing companies as described in the following case study.

sections.title: Mcdonald’S Corporation And Negative Book Value Of Equity

blocks.x: As of year-end 2013, McDonald’s Corporation (MCD) reported an all-time high book value of equity of over USD16 billion. However, by the end of 2016, the company’s book value of equity had fallen below zero. MCD’s book value of equity continued its decline until year-end 2019, reaching −USD8.2 billion and has continued to operate with negative book value of equity. While some companies experience negative equity book value due to net losses, MCD has enjoyed consistent profitability as its book value of equity fell from an all-time high to negative values. In fact, the company reported cumulative net income of over USD63 billion in net income between 2013 and 2023. However, the company paid USD39 billion in dividends and spent USD42 billion to repurchase shares over the same period. These cash distributions well above MCD’s net income drove its book value of equity downward. During this same period, MCD restructured its business by further increasing its focus on franchise operations and away from company-owned stores. The market value of MCD’s equity rose from USD96 billion at year-end 2013 to USD214 billion at year-end 2023, more than doubling despite the equity book value decline. Market Capitalization In contrast to historical balance sheet entries that comprise the book value of equity, a share’s market price reflects forward-looking investor expectations about future company cash flows generated by positive net present value investment opportunities. The product of the price per share and number of shares outstanding is a company’s market capitalization. (Market capitalization)t = Pt× (Shares outstanding)t.	                                (6) Unlike the book value of equity, changes in which are only observable when periodic financial statements are issued, this measure of the market value of a firm’s equity changes daily as share prices fluctuate. The number of shares outstanding may change within a financial reporting period due to issuance or buybacks and is available to market participants only once financial statements or other filings are released. Note that total shares outstanding include both those publicly held and available to trade as well as shares held privately or by management, such as restricted stock.
Knowledge Check

Eckwald AG’s (ECKW) finance department analysts are discussing the effect of a recent stock repurchase on the company’s book value and market value of equity. Eckwald repurchased four million shares at an average price of EUR125 on the last day of its most recent financial reporting period.

1. Describe the effect of ECKW’s stock repurchase on its book value of equity as well as on the market value of equity. Solution: The repurchase reduces ECKW’s equity in terms of both book value and market value. The book value of Eckwald’s equity declines by EUR500 million (= 4 million × EUR125) when the repurchase occurs, as this reflects the amount of capital distributed to shareholders. If the company repurchases shares at market value, this action should technically not affect the market price. However, the actual change in ECKW’s market value will depend upon the market’s interpretation of ECKW’s motivation to repurchase shares. On the one hand, it may signal management's confidence and belief that shares are undervalued, which may lead to a share price increase. Alternatively, the buyback may indicate a lack of investment opportunities, which may have a negative effect on the share price.

2. Explain the effect of ECKW’s stock repurchase on its market value and book value of equity as observed by an external equity analyst. Solution: Eckwald’s share repurchase on the final day of the reporting period is not transparent to investors as would be the case with dividends. The reduction in shares outstanding is only disclosed once Eckwald releases this information publicly. Thus, reported market capitalization will be based upon the prior period shares outstanding until that date. Unlike the decline in share prices on the ex-dividend date, share repurchases generally occur at market prices and do not coincide with observable share price changes. Once financial statements are released, an analyst should be able to isolate the effect of stock repurchases made during the prior financial reporting period. The time lag associated with the release of financial reports delays the ability of public analysts to observe the effects of ECKW’s repurchase activity.

The effect of share repurchases on market capitalization is more nuanced than the one-time ex-dividend day price change outlined in the prior learning module. As shown in the above exercise, share repurchases may occur on an opportunistic basis and are only disclosed to market participants after the fact. Changes in share price are not typically directly attributable to the cash outflow of the repurchase but rather by subsequent changes in market perception and financial statement disclosures. Beyond the timing differences and historical versus forward-looking nature of the book value of equity and market capitalization, investors often compare the two to draw initial conclusions about price versus value.
