Model Construction for Firms in Decline Many mature firms enter a stage of decline due to competitive forces, changing customer preferences and/or consumer tastes, technological change, or poor management, among other factors. Common features among these firms beyond falling sales, loss of market share, and lower profitability is a greater likelihood of financial distress, defined as the inability to meet future financial obligations to debtholders. Financial distress may result in the sale of the company to another firm or private investor, the restructuring of assets and liabilities under new management, or liquidation of the firm’s assets to pay its creditors. If asset sale proceeds are not sufficient to cover debts, shareholders face a total loss of their investment.

Despite such companies often having a long operating history over the economic cycle, use of either constant growth assumptions or financial models based on projecting existing financial statement relationships into the future may fail to fully capture the effects of potential financial distress. One approach is to adjust key areas of focus highlighted in Exhibit 19 when valuing firms in decline as follows:

• Cash flow adjustments. Analysts must identify and adjust key balance sheet and income statement items affected by a firm’s decline. For example, key customers or suppliers may switch to competitors or assets that are obsolete or substandard may face impairment. The timing and magnitude of these event-driven changes are uncertain.

• Denominator issues. Discount rates are difficult to estimate given the possibility of financial distress. Specifically, while the cost of debt is highly sensitive to the likelihood of default, the required return on equity will also vary widely as a company faces insolvency.

• Terminal value and forecast horizon issues. Future cash flow estimates imply that a firm will remain a going concern over the forecast horizon. Also, terminal value estimates based on multiples calculated using ratios from non-distressed industry peers will introduce distortion if a firm faces restructuring or liquidation. For a firm in decline, it may be preferable to incorporate the likelihood of financial distress more explicitly into valuation model construction, as described in Equation 14: IVt = Going-concern value × (1 − Prob(Distress))

(15) + Distress sale value × Prob(Distress). While Equation 14 is quite useful for firms in decline, the framework is reasonable to use for any firm for which future probability of business failure is a distinct possibility, as in the following example.

The Effect of Shareholder Control on Valuation Model Construction Equity investors may have a non-controlling, financial interest in a company or hold a larger stake seeking to control its activities. A financial investor is typically one who has no influence over a firm’s operations. When a company’s shares are widely held by financial investors or management, an analyst typically bases their valuation on how the firm is operated by its existing management. Changes in the composition of a company’s ownership, such as the emergence of a controlling investor, however, may signal significant changes that if anticipated may be incorporated into the disaggregated equity valuation approach. Controlling investors are often classified as strategic investors or activist investors. They may hold either a significant minority or majority stake and seek to initiate changes to increase shareholder value via seats on the board of directors, a majority shareholder vote, or by assuming full control of a firm and taking it private. These changes may include, but are not limited to, the sale of company assets, business combinations, and expense reduction or restructuring. When activist investors spell out their intentions to existing public shareholders seeking their vote in support of a restructuring plan, analysts can translate the proposed operating, investing, and financing changes into a detailed forecast for valuation purposes under a scenario in which these efforts are successful. The topic of corporate restructuring will be addressed later in the CFA® Program curriculum.

1. A valuation model for a company in the start-up phase of the company life cycle is most likely based on: A. a P/E multiple using expected earnings at the end of the forecast horizon. B. a P/S multiple using expected sales in the next year. C. a P/S multiple using expected sales at the end of the forecast horizon. Solution C is correct. Choice C is correct because an analyst valuing a start-up should apply a terminal value based on sales, not earnings, at the end of an expected high growth phase rather than in a year. Choice A is incorrect because the valuation model for a start-up is less likely to include earnings in an early phase than sales. Choice B is incorrect because the next year’s sales do not provide a complete picture of a start-up company’s full revenue growth potential.
2. Equity valuation models for start-up or growth companies are most likely to include terminal value estimates using: A. sales or earnings multiples. B. constant growth.

C. asset multiples. Solution A is correct. Choice A is correct because start-up and growth companies derive their value from revenue growth. As a result, terminal value estimates are most likely to be based on multiples of sales or earnings multiples. Choice B is incorrect because constant growth is a more likely assumption for mature companies rather than start-ups or growth firms. Choice C is incorrect because the use of an asset multiple would require a balance sheet forecast, which is less applicable to start-up or growth firms.

3. An analyst seeking to value the equity of a company that faces the possibility of financial distress is most likely to: A. increase the discount rate for future cash flows. B. incorporate the probability and value associated with distress. C. estimate a terminal value using non-distressed comparables. Solution B is correct. Choice B is correct because this approach captures the value of the firm as a going concern while incorporating the value if it experiences distress in the future. Choice A is incorrect because of the challenges associated with estimating the effects of distress on the costs of debt and equity. Choice C is incorrect because the terminal value estimation assumes the company is a going concern, distorting the analyst’s valuation.

The prior two lessons focused on financial model construction within an equity valuation process. In this lesson, we shift our focus to present a completed model in a step-by-step process. While the illustrations used in this lesson reflect numbers from a hypothetical company, the process shown generalizes to valuing any real-world company where historical financial statements are available and when an analyst invests time to build a narrative about possible outcomes.

Illustration of Equity Valuation To value equity using a disaggregated model, we follow a basic process described in the second lesson of this learning module. 1. Gather historical financial statements: 2. Construct an income statement forecast. 3. Construct a balance sheet forecast.

4. Use the forecasted financial statements to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics. 5. Estimate a terminal value associated with model outputs. 6. Compute a present value estimate from the free cash flows and terminal value. The essence of the valuation process occurs in the second and third steps above. The construction of income statement and balance sheet forecasts provides the inputs required to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics. Furthermore, the financial statement forecast narrative is likely to define how an analyst might estimate terminal value.

The analyst’s base case and optimistic scenarios both produce Folium equity value estimates that suggest significant equity price upside for the company’s stock from the current market capitalization of approximately EUR200 million. A key driver of the valuations in these two scenarios is profit margin improvement. Comparison of the base case and stable scenarios highlights this difference. Specifically, if Folium’s management is unable to improve EBIT margins significantly from 10.7% under the stable scenario, then the analyst’s assumed value improvements are questionable. Finally, the downside scenario implies that slowing revenue growth and declining

However, in this case, the market value of the firm’s debt would fall to a degree such that equity value remains positive (although it should be close to zero). These financial distress scenarios are addressed in detail later in the curriculum.

Interpretation of Scenario Valuation Results The analyst believes strongly that the base case scenario components reflect Folium’s revenue growth, profitability, and investment characteristics on a forward-looking basis. To signal strong confidence, the analyst applies a subjective 60% probability to this scenario. As the stable environment is believed to be the second most likely outcome, the analyst assigns a 20% probability to this valuation. Finally, the analyst assigns 10% probabilities to both the optimistic and pessimistic scenarios and their associated valuations.

1. If Folium’s equity is currently trading at EUR200 million, which one of the following is a likely conclusion about the analyst’s assessment of the company’s equity value? A. Folium’s equity is clearly undervalued. B. Folium’s equity is clearly overvalued. C. Folium’s equity is approximately fairly valued. Solution C is correct. Choice C is correct, as shown by the probability-weighted average of Folium’s equity value across the four scenarios: Folium equity value = 0.1 × 346.56 + 0.6 × 246.61 + 0.2 × 87.41 + 0.1 × 0 = 200.10. To account for the possibility that the downside scenario implies a Folium bankruptcy, an equity value of zero is assumed. Nevertheless, the probability-weighted average across the scenarios implies that Folium’s current equity value is in line with the analyst’s valuation scenarios and the subjective probabilities. Choice A is incorrect given the probabilities assumed by the analyst. Choice B is incorrect given the probabilities assumed by the analyst.

The exercise above illustrates that a company’s equity value reflects a range of possible future outcomes. The analyst assigns subjective probabilities to the discrete values associated with each scenario. However, the analyst’s subjective estimates of each scenario’s probability are unlikely to reflect the true, but unknowable, probabilities. In hindsight, only one scenario is realized, and market participants constantly reassess future possibilities as new information becomes available. As a result, financial statement models are updated as companies file quarterly or semiannual financial reports or other economic, market, or industry changes occur.

A More Detailed Set of Assumptions A second analyst assessing the original Folium equity valuation suggests that the assumption structure is too simplistic to properly reflect the company’s valuation. The analyst creates a new scenario to address these concerns. Exhibit 32 includes a more detailed set of assumptions as follows: 1. Separately consider COGS, SG&A, and D&A; 2. Separately consider working capital and net PP&E growth; 3. Incorporate a target debt ratio of 46%; 4. Allocate the financing surplus across cash, debt, and equity; and 5. Provide interest rates associated with borrowing and holding cash.

As a result, an analyst may have considered valuing Folium’s equity by assuming growth rates of its base year (t) free cash flows. 1. The analyst’s next step in valuing Veranta’s equity is to estimate a terminal value. Which one of the following best describes an analyst’s approach to terminal value estimation for Veranta? A. The analyst is likely to estimate Veranta’s terminal value using a constant growth model. B. The analyst is likely to estimate Veranta’s terminal value using a multiple applied to the company’s forecasted year t+5 sales or earnings. C. The analyst is likely to estimate Veranta’s terminal value using a multiple applied to the company’s forecasted year t+1 earnings. Solution B is correct. Choice B is correct because a relative valuation approach will be most appropriate for Veranta given the company’s continued growth trajectory with high revenue growth and improving margins. Choice A is incorrect because the constant growth model is most appropriate for estimating terminal value when the company has reached stability in its financial characteristics. That is not the case for Veranta as it is still expe-

riencing growth of 20% per year and its profit margins are likely to improve. Additionally, other characteristics also appear to lack stability. Overall, Veranta is likely not a good candidate for employing a constant growth model to estimate terminal value at year t+5 of its forecast. Choice C is incorrect because of two issues. First, Veranta has negative expected earnings in year t+1, so an earnings-based multiple will yield a negative result for the company’s value. Second, applying a multiple to a year t+1 forecast of earnings yields a current value estimate, not a terminal value.

1. Which one of the following statements most correctly describes equity valuation models using financial statement forecasts? A. Equity value is estimated using a free cash flow forecast calculated based on growth of a base year free cash flow. B. Equity value is estimated using a free cash flow forecast calculated from assumptions made about growth of financial statement items. C. Equity value is estimated including a terminal value estimated from base year earnings or revenues. Solution B is correct. Choice B is correct because the equity value reflects free cash flows calculated from the future financial statements constructed from an analyst’s assumptions about different components of financial statements, such as revenue growth, profit margins, investment, and financing needs. Choice A is incorrect because this statement implies an equity valuation in which an analyst does not construct a financial statement forecast. Rather, a base year free cash flow is constructed from historical financial statements, and forecasted free cash flows are simply computed from an analyst’s growth assumption. Choice C is incorrect because this statement incorrectly implies that an analyst estimates a terminal value from base year information. If, instead, terminal value is estimated from earnings or revenues from the final year of the financial statement forecast, this would be a more correct statement.

2. An analyst calculates a terminal value estimate using a constant growth model and uses this estimate to create a multiple of earnings. Which one of the following most correctly describes an advantage of converting this terminal value estimate into a multiple? A. The multiple may provide a way to assess the reasonableness of the terminal value estimate. B. The multiple ensures that the analyst has properly defined an appropriate peer group. C. The multiple provides a more appropriate methodology for calculating terminal value compared to a constant growth model. Solution A is correct. Choice A is correct because the analyst can compare the terminal value estimate multiple to a peer group multiple or to the company’s own multiple history to assess whether the multiple is economically reason-

able. As an example, a terminal value estimate that yields a P/E much higher than the P/E multiples of a group of comparables or the firm’s own historical P/E multiple would suggest that the constant growth model estimate should be re-estimated with differing assumptions. Choice B is incorrect because the analyst still needs to properly define an appropriate peer group. Simply converting the terminal value estimate into a multiple does not ensure that the analyst also identifies an appropriate peer group. Choice C is incorrect because the statement implies that the terminal value is initially calculated using a multiple (either from a peer group or from the company’s own history). However, this contradicts that the terminal value is initially computed using a constant growth model.

3. Vibria Company is a firm in a high growth phase of its life cycle, with revenue growth rates near 30% and negative profitability and cash flow. Analysts expect continued strong revenue growth and improving profitability for Vibria to continue for at least five years, by which time the company’s earnings are expected to be positive. Which of the following statements best describes a present value model for valuing Vibria’s equity? A. A five-year financial statement model to forecast Vibria’s free cash flows and a terminal value estimate generated by a constant growth model B. A five-year financial statement model to forecast Vibria’s revenues and a terminal value estimate generated by an assumed multiple of Year 5 revenues C. A five-year financial statement model to forecast Vibria’s free cash flows and a terminal value estimate generated by a multiple of forecasted Year 5 revenues or earnings Solution C is correct. Choice C is correct because the model described allows for the calculation of a positive terminal value estimate and also reflects the effect of negative free cash flows occurring during the forecast period of five years. Choice A is incorrect because a constant growth model requires both positive free cash flow and stability of the company’s financial fundamentals. In this case, insufficient information is provided as to whether the company is expected to be cash flow positive by the end of the five-year forecast horizon. If the company is still investing heavily to finance continued growth, it is plausible that investment may be greater than the company’s profitability. Choice B is incorrect because this describes a valuation derived solely from a revenue forecast. While such a process might be reasonable for a company in the start-up phase of the life cycle, this process is inadequate for a company in the growth phase.

sections.title: Summary: Financial Statement Forecasting In Equity Valuation

blocks.x: • Disaggregated valuation models allow an analyst to communicate a narrative associated with separate assumptions across financial statement forecasts of revenue, profitability, investment, and financing.
• Disaggregated models of revenue, expenses, and assets often rely on historical information and may involve bottom-up or top-down approaches to establishing a company’s financial statement forecast.
• The level of disaggregation used in constructing financial statement forecast models changes over a company’s life cycle. Companies at various stages are valued based on different forecast metrics.

• Analysts may incorporate the possibility that a company may face future financial distress using a probability-weighted average of a going-concern valuation and a bankruptcy or liquidation valuation.

• A basic process of company valuation involves the following steps: 1) gather historical financial statements; 2) construct financial statement forecasts over a future time horizon; 3) use the forecasted financial statements to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics; 4) estimate a forecasted terminal value associated with model outputs; and 5) compute a present value estimate from the forecasted free cash flows and terminal value.

B. Start-up company valuation models forego a near-term cash flow forecast and primarily focus on the firm’s expected future terminal value.

5. Which of the following statements best describes the key features of a disaggregated model for a growth company? A. Key equity value drivers in the growth phase include detailed revenue and profit projections to achieve targeted financial results.
B. Key equity value drivers in the growth phase include the level of earnings and the stability of earnings.
C. Key equity value drivers in the growth phase include the assumption of a constant growth rate and its use in estimating terminal value.

6. Which of the following statements best represents the process of how free cash flow metrics are estimated in a disaggregated forecast model for equity valuation purposes? A. Income statement and balance sheet forecasts provide the necessary inputs required to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics.
B. Assumed cash flow growth rates provide the necessary inputs required to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics.
C. Historical financial statements provide the inputs required to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics.
Solutions

1. C is correct. Choice C is correct because the increase in assumed dividend payout ratio for Years 3 and 4 causes assumed dividends per share to grow more rapidly than EPS during those two years. Choice A is incorrect because the dividend payout ratio remains at 40% for both years, so EPS and dividends per share are assumed to grow at the same rate in those two years. Choice B is incorrect because the dividend payout ratio remains at 40% in Year 2 before increasing in Year 3. As a result, EPS and dividends per share grow at the same rate in Year 2.

2. C is correct. Choice C is correct because the regression coefficient of 1.15 implies that the SG&A growth rate is faster than sales while the negative intercept term offsets the effect of growth. Thus, SG&A expense will be lower than sales growth only at lower sales growth rates. Confirming that this is true at 5% sales growth is shown below: SG&A growth rate = − 0.008 + 1.15 × 5 %   = 4.95%. Choice A is incorrect because the forecasted SG&A expense growth rate will only be higher than the sales growth rate at higher sales growth rates. As shown above, at a low growth rate of 5%, the forecasted SG&A expense growth rate is lower than the forecasted sales growth rate. Choice B is incorrect because the forecasted SG&A expense growth rate will be higher than the forecasted sales growth rate when it is 10%. Applying the same calculation as above yields a forecasted SG&A expense growth rate of 10.7% when sales growth is forecasted at 10%.

3. A is correct. Choice A is correct as shown in the calculations shown below. To answer the question, we use the following two equations: Financing needs = ∆ Operating assets − ∆ Non-debt liabilities − ∆ Retained earnings
FCFE = ∆ Cash + Dividends + Stock repurchases – Stock issuance

FCFE = − 2, 310 + 3, 220 + 0 – 0 = 910. Choice B is incorrect because the effect of the dividends are not considered in the financing needs calculation. However, the FCFE is correct because both dividends and change in cash are part of FCFE, and the payment of dividends is simply financed by drawing down the company’s cash balance in the correct solution above. Choice C is incorrect because FCFE does not incorporate the drawdown of the company’s cash balance to account for the financing needs.

4. B is correct. B is correct because start-up firms generate little to no near-term cash flow, with the full value often placed on the terminal value. A is incorrect, as start-up firms have little to no cash flow in their initial years of existence. C is incorrect, as constant growth assumptions are more appropriate for mature
firms.

5. A is correct. A is correct because growth companies focus on achieving scale and profitability over time via rapid growth. B is incorrect because growth firms often have low to no earnings and are seeking growth to achieve scale and targeted earnings over time. C is incorrect because growth firms typically are not expected to expand at a constant rate.

6. A is correct. A is correct because income statement and balance sheet forecasts provide the necessary inputs required to compute forecasted free cash flow metrics. B is incorrect because assumed cash flow growth rate inputs are used in present value models, not disaggregated forecast models. C is incorrect because while historical financial statements may form the basis for revenue, expense, and asset forecasts, they do not provide the inputs to compute free cash flow forecasts.

blocks.x: ANALYSIS | 1

The preceding Equities learning modules estimated intrinsic share value based on discounted cash flow, relative value, and disaggregated valuation modeling approaches. These quantitative tools based on forecasted income statement or balance sheet items should be substantiated by a detailed analysis of the business environment within which a firm operates and the risks it faces. In the next two learning modules, we turn our attention to industry and company analysis. This process should provide a consistent narrative supporting model results, completing the elements necessary for a thorough equity research report. This is likely to require iteration as an analyst refines the quantitative model to incorporate the most critical information obtained from industry and company analysis. The second lesson provides a basic overview of the steps involved in the process of industry and competitive analysis. Next, we address the classification of a firm within an industry and the associated challenges. We then highlight the process of surveying an industry’s size, growth, profitability, and composition to anticipate future industry and company trends. Finally, we revisit Porter’s Five Forces to assess the impact of industry structure and introduce PESTLE analysis to assess external factors affecting industry and company performance. The competitive strategy of a firm and evaluation of its past, present, and expected future performance will be the focus of the following learning module.

1. Which of the following represents a limitation of using third-party industry classification schemes? A. Currency differences B. Single-product companies C. Strict hierarchical taxonomies Solution: C is correct because commercial classification schemes, such as the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS), are examples of strict hierarchical taxonomies that classify companies into a single group, regardless of whether a firm offers products or services in different industries. A is incorrect because currencies have no impact on industry classification. B is incorrect because single-product companies are easily classified.

2. Which of the following statements best characterizes the difference between defensive and growth companies? A. Growth companies tend to be profitable across all phases of the business cycle, while defensive companies are not. B. Growth companies tend to expand revenue at above-trend rates across all phases of the business cycle, while defensive companies do not. C. Growth companies tend to acquire competitors across all phases of the business cycle, while defensive companies do not. Solution: B is correct because higher revenue expansion among growth companies tends to occur independent of the business cycle. A is incorrect because growth companies may or may not exhibit a high level of profitability depending on their stage of development, and their profitability is independent of the business cycle. C is incorrect because the distinction of growth versus defensive companies is related to business cycle sensitivity, not the acquisition of competitors.

3. Which of the following statements best characterizes the measurement of industry concentration using the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)? A. The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index is calculated as the sum of the squares of competitor market shares. B. The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index is calculated as the sum of squares of the number of competitors within an industry. C. The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index is calculated as the sum of the competitor market shares of the top four competitors in an industry. Solution: A is correct because the HHI is based on the sum of squares of market shares. A higher HHI indicates greater concentration. B is incorrect because the HHI is based on the sum of squares of market shares, not the number of industry competitors. C is incorrect because the HHI is based on the sum of squares of market shares for all industry participants, not just the top four companies.

4. Which of the following best characterizes the impact of profitability on an industry’s value creation? A. As a measure of excess return, the difference between an industry’s ROIC and its cost of equity is the best measure of profitability. B. As a measure of excess return, the difference between an industry’s ROIC and its WACC is the best measure of profitability. C. As a measure of excess return, the difference between an industry’s FCFE and its WACC is the best measure of profitability. Solution: B is correct because the ROIC reflects the return on capital and the WACC measures the cost of capital. Thus, the difference (or ratio) between ROIC and WACC reflects the excess return in an industry and is an effective measure of profitability. A is incorrect because the ROIC measures both debt and equity holder returns, while the cost of equity measures only shareholder return. C is incorrect because the FCFE measures shareholder return, while the WACC combines the cost of debt and equity.

5. Which of the following statements best describes the potential effect of an industry’s workforce as suppliers of labor under Porter’s Five Forces framework? A. The use of well-organized workers increases the bargaining power of suppliers within an industry. B. The use of well-organized workers increases the threat of substitutes within an industry. C. The features of an industry’s workforce is not a factor that is considered under Porter’s Five Forces framework. Solution: A is correct because the bargaining power of well-organized workers may force firms to pay higher wages or face competition among rivals in hiring and retaining these employees as suppliers of labor to firms in an industry. B is incorrect because the features of workers do not increase the threat of substitutes, as they are suppliers of labor to firms in an industry. C is incorrect because workers are considered to be suppliers with bargaining power.

6. Which of the following statements best describes the role of PESTLE analysis in industry and competitive analysis? A. PESTLE analysis seeks to better understand the threat of entrants in an industry or substitutes for its products and services. B. PESTLE analysis focuses on the bargaining power of suppliers and customers within an industry. C. PESTLE analysis focuses on the effect of external influences on an industry’s growth rate and market share dynamics. Solution: C is correct because the PESTLE framework considers external political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental influences on industry growth and market share changes.

A is incorrect because it describes two distinct elements included in Porter’s Five Forces analysis related to an industry’s competitive rivalry. B is incorrect because it lists two separate elements of Porter’s Five Forces analysis related to competitive forces within an industry.

Industry and competitive analysis provides the necessary context to both support the numerical inputs in an equity valuation model and establish a valuation narrative consistent with these inputs. The competitive opportunities, threats, and underlying value drivers faced by a firm are often shared by companies offering similar goods or services to customers that are grouped within an industry. Survey the Industry Once an analyst has determined the relevant scope of an industry, an important next step in gauging a firm’s potential growth and profitability is to gather data related to size, growth, and profitability and assess the existing composition of the firms included.

Porter’s Five Forces framework helps analysts understand influences affecting industry profitability. This framework was introduced in an earlier Economics learning module and is shown in Exhibit 3.

Porter’s Five Forces framework provides context and possible scenarios supporting a narrative on how an industry’s structure might change in the future. For example, consider the threat of entrants and substitutes in the Novo Nordisk example introduced earlier.
Example 2

Porter’s Five Forces and Novo Nordisk A/S As described in an earlier learning module, the Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk A/S established itself as a dominant player in diabetes and weight-loss solutions due largely to the success of Ozempic, a patented drug with approximately USD14 billion of revenue, which represented over 40% of its total 2023 revenue. Following its initial release in 2017 to treat diabetes, the observed weight loss in clinical trials led to the release of a higher-dose solution in 2021 to treat obesity. Although Novo Nordisk’s patented solution provided the company with an initial advantage over its rivals, challenges to its market dominance rapidly emerged. Given soaring demand, the company faced production constraints that limited its ability to fulfill customer orders. In the United States, the cost per patient was over USD900 per month before insurance reimbursement in 2023. Limitations on coverage of these costs by health insurance companies limited demand and created opportunities for lower-cost but less effective solutions. Key industry competitors, such as Eli Lilly, Pfizer, and Amgen, accelerated development of products similar to Ozempic, including Pfizer’s more attractive oral alternative to Novo Nordisk’s injectable therapy. Once Novo Nordisk’s patent expires in 2032, generic manufacturers can enter the market at lower prices. These forces are likely to erode Novo Nordisk’s market dominance, reducing its revenue and profitability over time.

Example 3

Government Health Care Policies and the Pharmaceutical Industry Because many governments regulate the practice of medicine, pharmaceutical firms producing prescription drugs depend on government approval for use, as well as reimbursement policies that make new therapies affordable for patients. For example, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires a lengthy preclinical and clinical research process to determine the efficacy and possible side effects of new drugs prior to sale. In the case of diabetes and weight loss solutions, Eli Lilly first applied for a patent for its antidiabetic medication tirzepatide in 2016, which was followed by three phases of clinical trials completed in 2021. The company received FDA approval for the use of tirzepatide as an antidiabetic therapy (sold as Mounjaro) in 2022 and as a weight loss medication under the name Zepbound in late 2023.
The external influence of government regulation in health care is an important determinant of the timing and magnitude of challenges to Novo Nordisk’s market dominance in this market.

Evaluate Competitive Strategy The final step in the industry and competitive analysis process considers the strategy of an individual firm in the context of its industry and its competitive advantage. This stage of the analysis is addressed in detail in the next learning module.

1. Which of the following represents the best approach in defining an industry? A. Use of Porter’s Five Forces analysis B. Use of a third-party classification scheme C. Use of the PESTLE framework Solution: B is correct because third-party classification schemes apply strict hierarchical taxonomies to categorize firms within a single industry group, regardless of whether a firm offers products and services in different industries. A is incorrect because Porter’s Five Forces analysis is used to explain industry profitability. C is incorrect because the PESTLE framework is used to explain the industry’s growth rate.

2. Which stage of the industry and competitive analysis process addresses the impact of environmental regulations on an industry? A. Porter’s Five Forces analysis stage B. Industry survey stage C. PESTLE framework stage Solution: C is correct because the PESTLE framework addresses external forces affecting an industry, such as political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental factors. A is incorrect because Porter’s Five Forces analysis addresses competitive forces within an industry, such as intercompany rivalry. B is incorrect because the industry survey stage involves estimating industry size, historical growth rate, and profitability and identifying company market share trends over time.
3. Which stage of the industry and competitive analysis process incorporates the threat of new entrants into the industry? A. Porter’s Five Forces analysis stage B. Industry survey stage

C. PESTLE framework stage Solution: A is correct because one of the five forces included in this stage is to analyze the threat of new entrants into the industry. B is incorrect because the industry survey stage involves estimating industry size, historical growth rate, and profitability and identifying company market share trends over time. C is incorrect because the PESTLE framework addresses external forces affecting an industry, such as political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental factors.
describe industry classification methods and compare methods by which companies can be grouped

An industry is commonly defined as a group of firms that offer comparable products or services from the perspective of a customer. The importance of such groupings for financial analysts is that such firms typically face similar competitive forces and value drivers. While this explains their use in establishing peer multiples for relative valuation purposes, described in an earlier learning module, industry analysis is an important element for all equity valuation approaches. The use of industry classifications provided by third parties enables analysts to consistently compare companies in the same sector. While the use of third-party classification aims to achieve uniformity in analysis and benchmarking, analyst discretion remains important, as described later in this lesson.

Third-Party Industry Classification Schemes Commercial classification schemes include the Global Industry Classification Standard, offered by MSCI and S&P Dow Jones Indices; the Industry Classification Benchmark (ICB), from FTSE Russell; and the Refinitiv Business Classification (TRBC), created by Refinitiv. These schemes group companies by the similarity of products and services offered, are global in nature, and are reviewed and updated at least annually, with new companies added more frequently. Schemes such as the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) and the European Nomenclature of Economic Activities (NACE) are also used within countries or regions. Exhibit 5 revisits the three major global classification schemes introduced in an earlier learning module.

Data aggregators (such as Bloomberg, FactSet, and S&P Capital IQ) and stock exchange operators (such as the London Stock Exchange) either use the industry classification schemes as shown in Exhibit 5 or have their own that are substantially similar. While each of the three classification schemes shown in Exhibit 5 has slightly different groupings, all are hierarchical taxonomies, with a company classified within a single group in the lowest tier, and the groups themselves making up the higher tiers. GICS, ICB, and TRBC have slightly different groupings, tiers, and names.

Limitations of Third-Party Classification Schemes While these classification schemes are a useful starting place for research and other uses, analysts face several key limitations when using such schemes to conduct industry research:
• Company groupings with significant business model variations or that sell substitute products
• Classification of companies operating in multiple industries
• Geographical considerations

• Changes in groupings over time affecting the comparability of statistics Analysts may find that industry groupings in the third-party schemes are either too narrow or too broad, as scheme providers use discretion in constructing groups based on product similarity and business model. In these cases, analysts may either apply higher or lower classification tiers or modify standardized groupings based on discretion and purposes of analysis. Industry classifications may in some cases involve significant variations in business models among firms, such as their ownership of real estate, as described in the following example.
Example 4

Real Estate Use at McDonald’s Inc. vs. Yum! Brands McDonald’s Corporation (MCD) and Yum! Brands, Inc. (YUM), are constituents within the Restaurant subindustry under the GICS industry classification within the Consumer Discretionary sector and the Hotels, Restaurants & Leisure industry. YUM has around 60,000 fast-food restaurants worldwide, as compared to over 40,000 for McDonald’s. That said, the two firms take different approaches to real estate in their business models. While both MCD and YUM have a very high percentage of franchised versus company-owned locations, McDonald’s owns a much higher proportion of the underlying real estate used by its restaurant operators, as evidenced by its balance sheet and income statement figures. For example, MCD has more than double the proportion of net property, plant, and equipment (PP&E) to total assets relative to YUM (68.4% versus 31.4% as of 2023). In addition, 63.7% of MCD’s gross PP&E is attributable to land and buildings and improvements on owned land, as opposed to only 3.5% for YUM. Given their global reach, the GICS, ICB, and TRBC classification schemes are more appropriate for the largest firms with recognizable brands that produce goods and services distributed worldwide. Firms operating in segmented national or local markets, however, may be less comparable under these industry classification schemes. This segmentation can arise due to customer behavior, transportation or other costs, or regulations that restrict competition. Differences in economic conditions, the degree of competition, or other factors across segmented markets reduce the comparability of companies, although they may offer the same products or services. For example, governments often regulate the practice of medicine through the licensing of facilities and physicians, as well as the provision of state-sponsored health care in certain countries. As a result, analysts typically consider the health care services industry on a national or regional rather than global basis. Finally, industry classifications may change over time. For example, GICS conducted a significant reclassification in 2023, including the shift of several firms, including Visa and Mastercard, from the Data Processing industry categorized within the Information Technology sector to Transaction and Payments Processing Services within the Financial sector. This is an example of classification changes affecting

industry groupings and statistics. Public offerings and delistings from acquisitions and bankruptcies also change the composition of the groupings over time, raising potential issues with historical return statistics. Analysts should use restated historical statistics that conform to the latest groupings and adjust for changes in the composition of groupings when possible.

Alternative Methods of Grouping Companies Industry or product-based approaches to grouping companies are not the only grouping methods and may be less useful in contexts outside industry analysis. Other approaches used include geography and business cycle sensitivity.

Geography Under this approach, companies may be classified by country, which are then aggregated by their stage of development, such as developed, emerging, and frontier markets. Country-based classification typically involves the country where the issuer is incorporated, the country of the primary listing of its equity securities, or the location of its headquarters. Companies operating within a specific jurisdiction may have more common value drivers because of political, economic, and social policies and conditions than companies offering similar products in other countries, as illustrated in the following example.
Example 6

The Nifty India Consumption Index An earlier Equities learning module described the Nifty India Consumption Index based on firms whose activities are primarily focused on domestic sales in India. This grouping of 30 companies publicly listed on the National Stock Exchange of India spans such industries as Consumer Non-Durable Goods, Health Care, Autos, and Media and Entertainment. While operating in different sectors, firms such as Hindustan Unilever Limited, a consumer goods manufacturer and majority-owned subsidiary of Unilever PLC, and Bajaj Auto Limited, a leading manufacturer of two- and three-wheel motorcycles for consumer transportation and delivery, may be more affected by the Indian consumer market than to global value drivers affecting their respective sectors.

It is important to note that a geographic classification typically does not consider the composition of a firm’s revenue or location of its assets, although these factors may be of importance to financial analysts for valuation purposes. For example, although Toyota Motor Company may fall under Japan using a geographic classification, its largest market by revenue is North America, which is also the location of most of its assets.

Business Cycle Sensitivity Firms are often classified as either cyclical companies or defensive companies based on the impact of economic fluctuations on their revenue and profitability. Cyclical companies are firms that experience greater fluctuations in revenue and profitability over the business cycle, while defensive companies are those whose sales growth, profitability, and valuations are less affected by changes in macroeconomic activity. Industries that supply, produce, and distribute discretionary goods and services or durable goods, such as housing, automobiles, appliances, and capital equipment, tend to be more cyclical. These products are generally long-lived, giving the buyer

flexibility as to when to purchase or replace them. Inputs for cyclical industries, including commodities, such as lumber, steel, and copper, and certain business services (e.g., heavy equipment rentals) also face demand fluctuations. For cyclical industries, revenue fluctuations result in greater operating profit fluctuations in the presence of high fixed costs. Defensive industries often include essential goods and services subject to inelastic demand, resulting in less revenue variation over the business cycle. This approach usually involves grouping entire sectors from the industry classification schemes discussed earlier. Defensive sectors include consumer staples, health care, and utilities; demand for their underlying products tends to remain stable over the business cycle. Cyclical firms involve the financial, basic materials, consumer discretionary, and industrial sectors. Growth companies are the third category of firms, which are relatively insensitive to the economic cycle. Firms within growth industries, which include those in such areas as emerging technology or biotechnology, generally exhibit rapid revenue growth regardless of the underlying economic environment, which may or may not be profitable, depending on their stage of growth. The key question for analysts considering investment strategies related to growth industries is how long the above-trend growth will persist and the level of profitability as the industry matures. Categorization based on business cycle sensitivity combined with a geographic approach may be advantageous when countries vary with respect to their position in the business cycle.

1. Which of the following statements best characterizes the treatment of companies operating in multiple industries under a strict hierarchical taxonomy? A. Strict hierarchical taxonomies classify these types of companies under more than one industry as reflected by their most important products and services by revenue. B. Strict hierarchical taxonomies classify these types of companies by the single largest product or service they offer in terms of revenue. C. Strict hierarchical taxonomies classify these types of companies in a separate category to reflect that they offer more than one product or service. Solution: B is correct because strict hierarchical taxonomies lead to the classification of companies in a particular group, regardless of whether a firm operates in multiple industries. A is incorrect because strict hierarchical taxonomies do not allow for inclusion of firms in more than one industry. C is incorrect because strict hierarchical taxonomies do not include a separate multiple industry company category.

2. Which of the following statements best characterizes the criterion used to group companies using a geographic approach? A. The location of most of their assets B. The country in which the company is incorporated

C. The country where the company generates most of its revenue Solution: B is correct because an issuer’s domicile is typically used to classify companies by geography, which may differ from the location of their assets or where they generate most of their revenue. A is incorrect because asset location is not a determinant of geographic classification. C is incorrect because the country that is the major source of a company’s revenue is not a determinant of geographic classification.

3. Which of the following statements best describes company groupings based on their sensitivity to the business cycle? A. In an economic downturn, defensive companies experience increases in revenue and profitability, while cyclical companies experience declines in revenue and profitability. B. In an economic upswing, defensive companies experience decreases in revenue and profitability, while cyclical companies experience increases in revenue and profitability. C. During periods of economic fluctuation, defensive companies experience more stability in revenue and profitability, while cyclical companies experience less stable revenue and profitability. Solution: C is correct because defensive companies experience more stability of revenue and profits, while cyclical company revenue and profitability fluctuate more over the economic cycle. A is incorrect since defensive companies experience more stable revenue and profitability during an economic downturn, not necessarily increases. B is incorrect because defensive companies experience more stable revenue and profitability during an economic upswing, not decreases.
determine an industry’s size, growth characteristics, profitability, and market share trends

Once an analyst has classified a company into an industry, the next step in the process is to survey the industry by estimating its overall size, determining its historical growth rate, evaluating the nature of that growth, measuring its profitability, and identifying major industry participants and market share trends over time. A firm’s industry market share is the percentage of total industry sales generated by the company over a specific period. This information on the current state of an industry establishes a basis for analysts to evaluate key issues and opportunities and project future trends using the frameworks on industry structure and external influences described in the following lesson.

Industry Size Two basic approaches exist in estimating the size of an industry: a top-down approach and a bottom-up approach. A top-down approach involves estimating total revenue across an entire industry over a given period. These data are typically compiled by a reputable third-party data provider or government statistical agency. For example, many governments track and publish periodic retail sales data. One shortcoming of this approach is that these data releases may not be granular enough to distinguish between retail industries supplying distinct types of goods and services. In contrast, a bottom-up approach involves the sum of the revenue generated by industry participants for specific goods or services for a given period. However, this does not necessarily correspond to the sum of revenue disclosures for all industry constituents. For example, an earlier example illustrated that Amazon.com is a participant in the supermarket industry. Simply adding Amazon.com’s total revenue, however, would include both its Amazon Web Services cloud computing business and its Whole Foods supermarket business, therefore overstating the size of the supermarket industry. An advantage of bottom-up analysis for industry groupings dominated by large, publicly traded companies with clear product and/or customer-based sales delineations is the ability to directly measure industry size. However, challenges may arise when an industry includes significant numbers of private companies with meaningful market share. Specifically, data for these industry participants may be limited or unavailable. Also, when companies operating in multiple industries are involved, differences in segment breakdowns and how companies disclose operating segments may require analysts to make estimates based on forms of disclosure outside of a firm’s audited financial statements. When information challenges make industry-wide figures impractical or impossible to calculate using firm-specific data, it is common practice to estimate industry size using a top-down approach, whether this includes economic indicators published by government agencies, data from third-party consultancies that conduct surveys, or industry data from issuers’ investor presentations based on proprietary sources. For example, it is best to estimate the size of an industry that includes thousands of small businesses using figures published by a government agency, as described in the following example.

Industry Growth Characteristics An industry’s pattern of historical growth is usually compared to broader economic measures of activity over time and should be evaluated over the cycle to gauge an industry’s sensitivity to economic fluctuations. Since growth in all industries in aggregate should technically equal macroeconomic growth, we would expect more mature industries that have reached their addressable market and potential customers to grow at a rate near or below that of

the economy. Key issues for investors in a mature industry include monitoring for disruptive threats, changes in competitive intensity, and the potential onset and speed of decline. Sensitivity to the business cycle tends to be higher for industries involving discretionary sales, consumer durable or capital goods, or companies whose revenue is exposed to the interest rate cycle. Expansion rates in growth industries usually exceed that of the economy and are usually not sensitive to business cycles, because they have not yet reached full penetration of their total addressable market. Key questions for analysts related to growth industries include the length of time over which above-trend growth will persist and the expected peak penetration rate, which are more difficult to estimate in earlier stages of growth. Industry growth rates may be affected by structural changes affecting the demand for certain products and services or by more severe economic shocks. For example, the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on industry growth is described in the following example.
Example 7

Industry Growth Rates during the COVID-19 Pandemic The unprecedented restrictions on economic activity and free movement in public spaces that began in early 2020 as governments sought to limit the spread of COVID-19 had a profound negative effect on industry growth in many sectors, while having a positive impact on others. For example, sectors dependent on travel and the in-person delivery of goods and services faced severe setbacks due to travel bans, economic lockdowns, and quarantines. Global passenger air travel fell by 60% in 2020, while the sharp growth in e-commerce during the same period increased global air freight yields by 30% during the same year. The decline in both road traffic and passenger air travel had an adverse effect on the oil and gas industry amid rising inventory and falling prices. According to the International Energy Agency, primary energy demand fell by 4% in 2020. Half of the decline was attributable to decreased automobile traffic, and over a third was due to the drop in passenger air travel. Industries and firms within industries that benefited from the pandemic because of the same economic forces included cloud computing, videoconferencing applications, and industries with internet-based business models, such as streaming services and online shopping. For example, while overall US retail sales fell slightly in 2020, e-commerce sales jumped by over 30% over the same period.

Measuring Value Creation in the Passenger Airline Industry The prior example illustrated global passenger airline industry exposure to economic shocks. As shown in the prior learning module using the case of Deutsche Lufthansa, airlines exhibit significant cyclicality in revenues and expenses, with costs that are driven in part by volatile jet fuel prices and revenue dependent on both business and premium travelers, which can fluctuate over the business cycle, as well as leisure travel, which is dependent on disposable income. Given these industry features, it is important to consider whether passenger airlines are able to create value over the business cycle. Exhibit 9 uses data compiled from Bloomberg on the ratio of ROIC to WACC from a sample of passenger airlines, including Delta Airlines, United Airlines, IAG Group (the parent company of British Airways, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, among others), Deutsche Lufthansa, and Air France, over a 15-year period to estimate excess accounting returns in the airline industry over this time period. The red dashed line is set at a ratio of exactly 1, and years above (below) this benchmark indicate positive (negative) excess returns.
Exhibit 9: Average ROIC/WACC for Selected Airlines, 2009–2023
Average ROIC/WACC

Source: Bloomberg. As shown in Exhibit 9, the airline industry generated returns that were below its cost of capital following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, reaching positive excess returns for a single year (2011) before oil price spikes over the following

years eroded profit margins despite a recovery in passenger demand. While the industry as a whole enjoyed positive excess returns over a five-year period thereafter, the COVID-19 pandemic had a severe negative effect on ROIC, leading to negative returns until 2022.

While the earlier example shows how an industry as a whole may or may not create value over time, variations among industry participants indicate the dispersion of value creation across companies in the same sector. For example, in 2014 as global oil prices fluctuated near USD100 per barrel, US-based carriers Delta and United generated ROIC well in excess of WACC, while their European-based industry competitors did not. Challenges in obtaining and evaluating these profitability measures arise if there is a substantial number of private companies in an industry. The following are two common methods to overcome this challenge in practice to estimate industry profitability:
• Measure the profitability of publicly traded industry constituents and assume that the private company’s profitability is similar.

• Obtain data from a government agency or third-party consultancy. For example, the same government agency that publishes retail sales data also conducts an annual survey of retailers’ gross margins and operating expenses, which may be used to calculate retail industry operating margins. As in the case of industry revenue, changes in profitability over time as compared to growth in the overall economy shed light on an industry’s sensitivity to the overall business cycle.

Market Share Trends and Major Industry Participants Industry market shares are measured by dividing each participant’s annual revenue by total industry revenue. Given the challenges in measuring industry size mentioned earlier, market shares should be interpreted as a range rather than a point estimate. Significant changes in market share or emerging new industry participants are indicative of the potential for intensive competitive rivalry, as described in the following lesson. The degree of industry concentration is an essential element of an industry survey. The lower the industry concentration, the greater the competitive intensity, unless an industry is segmented or has a high level of product differentiation. Rising industry concentration or consolidation is generally associated with falling competitive intensity and higher profitability. A common measure of industry concentration is the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index, calculated as the sum of the squares of competitor market shares: n

where s is the market share of market participant i stated as a whole number (i.e., 50% share = 50, not 0.50).

It is important to consider the effect of mergers and acquisitions on market share, as well as whether a company has a rising or falling market share on an organic (non-acquired) basis, as discussed in the following example.
