Given the degree of estimation required to gauge an industry’s size, growth characteristics, profitability, and/or market share trends, it is often important to substantiate measures of industry and competitive analysis using more than one approach. As the prior knowledge check shows, even quantitative measures of competitive intensity, such as HHI calculations, are sensitive to analyst assumptions.

1. Which one of the following statements best characterizes the measurement of an industry’s size? A. An appropriate bottom-up approach to measuring industry size is to simply add up the total revenue figures of all firms in an industry.

B. Economic indicators published by government agencies, data from third-party consultants, or industry data may be used in a top-down approach to estimating industry size. C. Estimated consumer expenditure on specific goods or services over a specific period may be used in a top-down approach to estimating industry size. Solution: B is correct because government economic indicators, consultant data, or industry data may be used to estimate industry size in a top-down approach. A is incorrect because it fails to account for firms that operate in multiple industries and private companies that may not release revenue information. C is incorrect because the basis for measuring industry size is total revenue, not customer spending.

2. Which of the following approaches best characterizes the relationship between an industry’s growth rate and the overall economy? A. Industries growing more slowly than the overall economy are in decline. B. Industries with less cyclical growth than the overall economy are mature. C. Industries that are relatively insensitive to business cycles are growth industries. Solution: C is correct because growth industries are insensitive to business cycles, since they have not yet reached full saturation of customer demand or penetration of their total addressable market. A is incorrect because mature industries may also grow but at a slower rate than the economy since the aggregate of all industries constitutes the overall growth rate. B is incorrect because mature industries may be cyclical or defensive.

3. Which of the following statements best addresses the impact of market share concentration in an industry? A. The fewer firms competing in an industry, the higher the Herfindahl– Hirschman Index will be for that industry. B. The fewer firms competing in an industry, the higher the competitive intensity will be in that industry. C. The fewer firms in an industry, the less likely that regulatory authorities will prevent a merger that consolidates industry participants. Solution: A is correct because the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index is equal to the sum of squares of industry participant market share, which increases as the number of firms competing in an industry declines. B is incorrect because fewer firms in an industry reduces the competitive intensity of that industry. C is incorrect because mergers that consolidate market share and reduce competition in an industry are more likely to be scrutinized and challenged by regulatory authorities.

sections.title: Porter’S Five Forces And The Pestle

blocks.x: FRAMEWORK | 5
analyze an industry’s structure and external influences using Porter’s Five Forces and the PESTLE framework

The prior lesson established the size, growth, profitability, and composition of companies grouped in an industry based on historical information. As a next step in completing a thorough forward-looking analysis of an industry and the companies in an industry, it is critical to evaluate the dynamic forces operating within an industry, as well as external factors that influence its growth and profitability.

The Use of Porter’s Five Forces in Equity Analysis Recall from an earlier Economics learning module that Porter’s Five Forces framework was used to assess industry structure. As shown previously in Exhibit 3, these forces are as follows:
• Threat of entrants
• Threat of substitutes
• Bargaining power of customers
• Bargaining power of suppliers

• Rivalry among existing competitors If some or all of these five industry forces are intense, industry return on capital is unlikely to exceed the cost of capital. This is consistent with earlier Economics learning modules that described firms in perfectly competitive markets in which the price of products and services is equal to marginal cost. Less intense industry pressures, in contrast, often lead to highly profitable industries. In the previous lesson, we considered an industry’s profitability on a historical basis, whether it is a source of value creation, and how this value creation is distributed among its participants. For new industries with little or no data or that are still in an early, unprofitable stage, this industry structure analysis can help point to the likelihood, timing, and level of potential future profitability. Using the analogy of a water-filled trench surrounding a fortified castle, such investors as Warren Buffett have described a long-standing competitive advantage as an economic moat. The wider the moat, the greater the potential to sustain profitability in excess of capital costs over longer periods. A wide moat may exist for all the firms in an industry with fewer constituents, such as an oligopoly. Alternatively, economic moats may be present for just one or two profitable firms among many in a highly competitive industry whose returns as a whole fall short of the WACC. While factors affecting the moats vary widely across industries and companies, analysts and data providers have sought to distill and apply this information in the investment selection process as described in the following example.
Example 10

Morningstar’s Economic Moat Rating The US-based investment research and ratings firm Morningstar, Inc., created a proprietary rating system designed to gauge the relative size of a company’s economic moat using the following criteria:
• Intangible assets
• Switching costs
• Network effect
• Cost advantages

• Efficient scale For example, VanEck, a US-based investment management firm that operates globally, has established exchange-traded funds (ETFs) using security selection based on Morningstar’s economic moat rating of a firm.
In what follows, we align factors such as those affecting the relative width of an economic moat with Porter’s Five Forces to address how analysts evaluate the competitive rivalry within an industry.

Assessing the Threat of New Entrants The evaluation of market share trends from the prior section is an important first step in determining how new competitors will affect an industry. Beyond the number of entrants over a specific period, their impact on industry incumbents is an important determinant of future competitive rivalry. For example, the acquisition of startups by technology firms, such as Alphabet’s acquisition of YouTube or Meta’s purchase of WhatsApp, serves to neutralize the threat of new industry entrants on industry incumbents. In other cases, entrants such as Tesla in the automotive industry pose an enduring threat to existing automotive manufacturers. Incumbent responses to these threats include partnerships with new entrants to combat the competitive threat, as in the case of electric vehicles described next.
Example 11

Volkswagen AG’s Joint Venture with Rivian Automotive, Inc. Volkswagen AG, the world’s second-largest auto manufacturer, based in Germany, and US-based electric vehicle (EV) producer Rivian Automotive announced a USD5.8 billion joint venture in November 2024. Volkswagen built a strong engineering reputation over many decades with its traditional internal combustion engine technology, but the auto industry’s shift to EVs created competitive challenges for the company. While Rivian proved to be an effective innovator in computing and software technology in the EV space, it lacked the cash to capitalize on these developments by increasing its production scale. The joint venture allows Volkswagen to gain direct access to the technology necessary to upgrade its vehicles to the digital age. While Rivian and VW will each have a 50% stake in the new venture, Volkswagen will contribute capital and fund 75% of the shared platform costs, while Rivian will fund the remainder.

Government regulation may limit or prohibit entry into an industry in some cases, such as for investor-owned regulated utilities granted the right to supply power, gas, or water in a specific region. In other cases, regulation may function as a barrier to entry given the cost of complying with regulations that only larger companies can afford. Other forms of entry prevention include government subsidies for domestic firms or restrictive licensing requirements. The case of patents involves a temporary barrier to market entry, granting firms the exclusive right to develop new products or technologies, while preventing competitors from providing the same offering until the patent expires. In this case, financial analysts must assess the value of a competitive advantage over a finite patent protection period, as described next.
Example 12

Pfizer’s Competitive Advantage in Lowering Cholesterol Atorvastatin, branded as Lipitor, is a cholesterol-lowering drug developed by Pfizer Inc., a US-based multinational pharmaceutical firm. First developed in 1985, clinical trials of the drug progressed until the company received exclusive patent protection from 1997 until 2011. Lipitor generated substantial revenue for Pfizer, peaking at USD12.9 billion in 2006 annual sales and resulting in over USD125 billion in cumulative sales for Pfizer over the period of patent protection. While atorvastatin remains among the most highly prescribed medications in developed countries, Pfizer experienced a revenue drop of over 50% from the drug once patent protection expired as generic drug manufacturers entered the market and eliminated the company’s competitive advantage.

The previous case highlights an important feature of the non-generic pharmaceutical industry—specifically, the importance of continuous research and development of a new generation of patent-protected drugs. Analysts researching an industry must develop a strong understanding of these industry dynamics and their effect on company fundamentals. Preventing the threat of entry over an indefinite period may include some or all of the factors described in an earlier example related to the width of an economic moat, including the following:

• Intangible assets: In addition to the value of patents, brands that command customer loyalty represent a barrier to entry to firms that may vary widely across industries. While the value of the Lipitor brand failed to protect Pfizer’s revenue when generic drugmakers entered the market, consumer luxury brands and brands in the food and beverage industry benefit from faithful customers.

• Switching costs: Costs or expenses faced by a customer when changing from one product or service can serve as a substantial barrier to entry unless the perceived long-term benefits of switching far outweigh the near-term costs. These costs may include opportunity costs, risks associated with new firms or products, and expectations of upgrades from existing providers. For example, switching business software providers (such as from SAP to Salesforce) often requires lengthy implementation processes led by third-party consulting firms and establishing connectivity to other internal software applications, which is often a costly and lengthy process. In contrast, switching service providers who use a smartphone app presents no limitations due to switching costs.

• Network effect: As described in an earlier Economics learning module, a network effect involves a situation in which the value of a product or service grows as adoption by households and/or businesses increases. The large demand-side economies of scale associated with the network effect of an established firm in an industry limits the ability of new entrants to compete, despite the potential benefits of a new product or service. The economic benefits to industry incumbents with strong network effects depends on the degree to which a provider can monetize the network, which often increases as network usage grows. Key examples include social media platforms, such as Meta, and payment systems, including Visa and Mastercard. While advertising revenue supports most social media platforms, volume-based transaction and other fees for data processing generate revenue for payment platforms, which grows in value to end users as the network expands.

• Cost advantage: Firms that are able to provide goods or services to customers at a lower cost have a pricing advantage over new entrants. Cost advantages usually arise in combination with one or more additional sources of competitive advantage, such as proprietary technology, brand loyalty, or scale. In other cases, incumbents benefit from economies of scope across multiple products. Economies of scope arise when the cost of producing two or more distinct goods or services is less than that of producing each separately. Examples include the bundling of cable television, wi-fi connectivity, and telephone service with one provider.

• Efficient scale: Efficient scale markets are industries that typically face mature demand for a commoditized product with inelastic demand and high entry costs. In these cases, entrants lack the incentive to enter a market in which additional capacity would drive returns below the cost of capital. Examples include the freight railway industry, in which the cost of maintaining rail infrastructure is very high, while the market attains efficiency through supporting a few operators on a shared rail network.

Assessing the Threat of Substitutes The threat of substitutes rises when another product or service becomes available that fulfills the same or similar customer need as an existing product, particularly when offered at a lower price. In some cases, the threat of substitutes may arise across seemingly different industries. The following example describes the competitive rivalry among small and large videoconferencing application providers.
Example 13

Videoconferencing Application Substitutes While the use of videoconferencing applications soared more than thirtyfold during 2020, the competitive rivalry among firms offering this service, including Slack Technologies, Zoom Video Communications Inc., Microsoft Corporation, and Alphabet Inc., began prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. Slack and Zoom represented small, innovative players in the market. As a collaboration pioneer, Slack positioned itself as a customizable platform with a focus on integration with third-party applications. Salesforce Inc. acquired Slack in 2021, allowing its integration with customer relationship management software. Despite the advantage of integration with thousands of third-party apps, Slack is text focused, with weaker video capabilities. Zoom launched its meeting video software in 2013 and went public in 2019. It is known for superior

video and audio quality, a user-friendly interface, and scalability. Zoom was a dominant video conferencing provider during the pandemic but has since faced competition from more established rivals. As larger market participants, Microsoft and Google have added video conferencing features to existing platforms. Microsoft Teams was launched in 2017 and became a top choice for many organizations given its integration within the Microsoft 365 offering, combining chat and file sharing collaboration tools with videoconferencing. Google Meet was also launched in 2017 and is integrated with the Google Workspace ecosystem, such as Gmail and Google Drive.

Although competition among videoconferencing providers continued as the COVID-19 pandemic subsided, these applications also substitute for in-person meetings and office work, reducing the need for business travel and commercial office space capacity, while expanding opportunities in such areas as remote education and telemedicine.

Assessing the Bargaining Power of Suppliers and Customers Beyond the threat of industry entrants and substitutes for the goods and services produced in an industry, a thorough analysis must also consider the impact of an industry’s suppliers and customers on competitive rivalry. The bargaining power of suppliers can vary widely across industries. This power is in general positively correlated with the concentration of available suppliers to an industry, the degree to which the materials or components required are unique or tailored to a specific firm, and the cost of switching providers. When few concentrated providers supply inputs to a specific firm or industry, their bargaining power can be very high. As an example, Apple Inc., the world’s largest purchaser of semiconductor chips for its smartphones and other devices, buys all of its advanced chips from TSMC, the leading multinational semiconductor contract manufacturing and design firm. While Apple is beholden to TSMC for its advanced semiconductor chips, it has retained control of the designs and intellectual property for these components in its devices. The effect of supplier concentration is not limited to material inputs, because the licensing of proprietary technology or intellectual property can have similar effects on bargaining power and the competitive rivalry among industry participants. Examples include the licensing for certain chip designs in the semiconductor industry and streaming content such as live sports or popular entertainment among media content providers. The presence of switching costs is an additional factor affecting the bargaining power of suppliers. In the case of both semiconductors and index providers, the typically high cost of changing suppliers contributes to their market power. In the case of semiconductors, switching the source of this critical input represents a strategic change that may require product changes and significant investments and time, while ETF issuers that commonly feature the name of a benchmark index in their product offering and compare their funds against others using a similar index might jeopardize the comparability of their offering if switching to an alternative index. The supply of specialized workers in an industry may also affect the competitive rivalry within the industry if the necessary labor is highly skilled, requires licensing, or is well organized. For example, the bargaining power of unionized factory workers may force firms to negotiate wage increases that are favorable to workers. Labor strikes are a disruptive force among manufacturing companies and transportation companies, such as commercial airlines. In contrast to industries with few specialized suppliers and high switching costs, supplier bargaining power is at its lowest in industries with many small-scale providers of commoditized inputs that may be easily substituted. Examples include retail

industry segments, such as clothing or housewares, that sell private-label products; low-tech manufacturing with a high interchangeability of components; or restaurants or food service businesses. In cases where industry participants are large buyers of inputs, they have the power to exert considerable influence over suppliers in terms of pricing, quality standards, delivery times, and payment terms. The relative bargaining power of an industry’s customers depends on the features of the underlying product or service and the nature of the industry’s customer base. Highly commoditized products and services, or those for which switching costs are extremely low, are common among industries where customers have a high degree of bargaining power. This power drives competition among industry participants in the form of price competition, product differentiation, bundling of services, or other strategies to increase customer loyalty. By rewarding more frequent customers with incentives, such as discounts, frequent flyer miles, or other exclusive offers, these firms attempt to overcome the low switching costs related to their products and services. The following example describes these strategies in the case of convenience stores.
Example 14

Competitive Strategies in the Convenience Store Industry Convenience stores occupy a distinct space in the food retailing industry given their smaller store size in high traffic areas designed to meet the more frequent, everyday needs of consumers making small, ready-to-eat purchases at premium prices compared to standard grocery stores. Consumers also often have a wide range of substitutes when weighing a decision to shop at these stores. This segmented market is composed of both small domestic and large global private and public firms across sectors, including food retail and oil and gas. For example, major global competitors range from the privately held Japanese Seven & I Holdings to the publicly held French food retailer Carrefour S.A., British multinational oil and gas giant British Petroleum, and Alimentation Couche- Tard (ATD), a publicly held Canadian operator of convenience stores in over a dozen jurisdictions worldwide. Whether located in central business districts, congested suburban areas, or along highways, these stores use a range of strategies to bundle offerings and grow their numbers of repeat customers. For example, ATD’s Circle K stores offer a loyalty program in which customers earn points for purchases and special rewards for fuel purchases that are redeemable for free discounted items. Subscription-based programs to save on fuel costs or offer unlimited coffee or tea for a monthly fee promote returning customers. Use of the company’s mobile app allows users to track reward points, search for company locations, and access personalized offers, as well as pre-order items and pay via the company’s app.

In other cases, a large and concentrated customer base for an industry’s products or services often significantly increases customers’ bargaining power over suppliers within an industry. As described earlier, when few large buyers use an industry’s output, they have a greater ability to dictate pricing, quality standards, delivery times, and payment terms. While outsourcing remains a common strategy in the manufacturing sector, a key competitive strategy often used in industries that face a high degree of supplier or customer bargaining power is vertical integration. Vertical integration involves the expansion of operations into an earlier or later stage of the production or supply chain associated with the delivery of a product or service to end users.

Expansion of a firm’s activities to an earlier stage of the production process is commonly referred to as upstream or backward integration, in which a firm or group of firms within an industry seek to take control of suppliers or raw material production. This control can be in the form of exclusive supplier agreements, joint ventures as described in the earlier example of Volkswagen and Rivian, or outright ownership of resources or production facilities. The example of rare mineral inputs and battery production for electric vehicles is illustrated next.
Example 15

Electric Batteries and the Automaker Supply Chain The shift from internal combustion technology to battery-powered electric vehicles has had a significant impact on the automotive industry supply chain. The most valuable component of pure EVs, electric batteries, represents over a third of total vehicle value. Critical minerals, such as lithium, cobalt, manganese, nickel, and graphite, are refined and processed to create the electrodes that form the basic building block of EV batteries. Given that the supply chain of minerals for EV batteries is concentrated in the Chinese Mainland, global automakers have taken steps to diversify their sources of this critical production input. For example, when US-based EV automaker Tesla, Inc., began its mass production of battery-powered passenger cars in 2014, it was solely reliant on batteries supplied by Panasonic Corporation. As the company reached a higher scale of production, it pursued upstream integration by directly partnering with mining companies to secure lithium, nickel, and other battery-grade minerals and partnering with Panasonic in research and technology to initiate its own battery production at its Gigafactory in 2016. While Tesla continues to expand its battery production capacity at Gigafactory facilities worldwide, it continues to partner with Panasonic, as well as South Korea–based LG Energy Solutions and Chinese Mainland battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), to meet its global battery needs. Traditional US automakers, such as General Motors Company and Ford Motor Company, have taken similar steps to ensure access to key EV battery raw materials and entered joint ventures to secure EV battery production capacity. For example, in 2019, GM and LG Energy Solutions entered into a joint venture, Ultium LLC, to jointly build EV batteries in the United States. Ford Motor Company, in contrast, entered an agreement to partner with CATL in which it retains full ownership of new US-based battery manufacturing facilities while licensing CATL’s technology.

In the prior example and other cases of backward integration, firms in an industry must weigh the reduced dependence on external parties and scarce resources with significant upfront investments and reduced flexibility resulting from expanding operations across the supply chain. The alternative to upstream integration involves a shift towards eliminating intermediaries, such as distributors, retailers, or other providers that interact directly with end users of a firm’s products or services. As described in the following example, this allows a firm to extract a higher proportion of the value chain associated with the final purchase price of goods and services, improve efficiency, or take advantage of scale in order to offer a more integrated customer experience.
Example 16

Amazon Prime and Downstream Integration Amazon.com initiated a USD79 annual membership in 2005 for US customers that offered two-day free shipping of the company’s products. As the company broadened its member services and added customers, it made major investments in fulfillment centers, vehicles, and air cargo services in order to establish its own logistics and delivery network, competing directly with shipping industry incumbents, such as Federal Express (FDX) and United Parcel Service (UPS). Amazon expanded its Prime membership services to include music and film streaming while increasing its global reach. In 2022, the company surpassed both UPS and FDX in US delivery volume, and it generated over USD20 billion in membership fees alone in the first half of 2024, with over 200 million members in 25 countries.

Assessing Rivalry among Existing Competitors In addition to the ease of industry entry, substitutes, and the bargaining power of suppliers and customers, analysts consider a number of other factors when assessing industry rivalry, including the following:
• Price competition
• Product differentiation
• Relative size of major competitors and market share changes

• Industry growth rates and profitability As an analyst completes the evaluation of industry structure, it is important to highlight the relative influence of these factors on competitive rivalry. While no definitive assessment exists by which to gauge their relative importance, a thorough analysis allows for the incorporation of scenarios in which one or more factors may dominate the others under different circumstances. Consider the following example based on the passenger airline industry from an earlier example.
Example 17

Porter’s Five Forces Analysis for the Passenger Airline Industry Threat of New Entrants: Low to Moderate Potential entrants in the passenger airline industry face significant capital investment requirements, with industry incumbents benefiting from economies of scale. Such regulatory hurdles as strict aviation regulations and licensing requirements in some markets serve as deterrents to new industry entrants. While established global airlines benefit from extensive networks and frequent flyer programs, in some regions or markets, low-cost carriers (LCCs) have a lower entry barrier due to flexible leasing options, limited schedules, and the use of secondary airports. As a result, the threat of entry is low for major global carriers but moderate for LCCs in many regional and underserved markets.

Threat of Substitutes: Moderate While driving and high-speed rail travel represent substitutes for short-haul passenger air travel, long-haul flights have few alternatives. Business-related travel remains affected by remote work trends and virtual meetings, as described

in an earlier example. However, few alternatives to air transportation exist for leisure travel and tourism. As a result, substitutes for passenger air travel are a moderate threat and are more pronounced for shorter trips and business-related travel, while longer flights and leisure travel are less susceptible to substitution.

Bargaining Power of Suppliers: High Passenger airline companies are dependent on aircraft manufacturers, fuel deliveries, and unionized employees as key suppliers. The global dominance of jet aircraft manufacturers Boeing and Airbus leave airlines with little bargaining power. As a major expense item for passenger airlines, oil prices are subject to significant volatility, which affects operating margins. Airline pilots, engineers, and maintenance workers are often well organized, affording them the ability to negotiate wage and benefit increases, driving up airline operating expenses. Airlines are heavily dependent on these suppliers, which have strong bargaining power due to their critical role in operations and the lack of substitutes. Bargaining Power of Customers: High Passenger airline customers are very sensitive to price differences, which are highly transparent given the widespread practice of online travel booking. While airlines use such strategies as branded credit cards, frequent flier programs, premium seating, and travel lounge access, customer loyalty is limited given low switching costs, particularly for short-haul trips and popular destinations. Demand for non-essential air travel is also sensitive to the business cycle. Business travelers may face constraints due to restrictive travel policies, limit travel in economic downturns, and may forgo travel altogether in favor of remote meetings as described earlier. Leisure travelers may delay discretionary holiday travel or substitute ground travel for flights when seeking to limit expenses. As a result, customer bargaining power in the passenger airline industry is considered high.

Intensity of Competitive Rivalry: High A high degree of industry rivalry results from numerous global and regional airlines and low-cost carriers competing on price, routes, and service quality while facing high operating expenses and suppliers with significant bargaining power. Regulatory constraints limit the degree of industry consolidation, while barriers to exit may lead to greater price competition during economic downturns. As illustrated in an earlier example, the airline industry faces cyclical demand and returns below the cost of capital over the cycle, intensifying the rivalry among competitors.

The relative importance of these industry factors may also be influenced by external factors that play a role in the valuation process, such as the likelihood of an economic downturn or higher and more volatile oil prices. We now turn our attention to these elements and their effect on industry and competitive analysis.

PESTLE Framework While Porter’s Five Forces analysis seeks to better explain the competitive rivalry among firms within an industry, factors driven by forces outside an industry often affect future growth prospects and the relative market positions of individual firms within the industry based on their ability to anticipate and adapt to changing conditions. The PESTLE framework, which analyzes political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental influences on an industry, is a common approach. While Porter’s Five Forces pertain to the determinants of industry profitability, PESTLE

analysis is more concerned with an industry’s growth rate and market share dynamics based on these influences. Analysis of these external forces helps analysts identify themes or narratives that may be incorporated into the equity valuation process with a positive or negative influence on an industry or companies within an industry. For example, the COVID-19 pandemic had a profound, immediate adverse effect on such sectors as transportation and physical retail, while accelerating the digitalization of payments. Long-lasting effects of COVID-19 include the trend toward remote work, which affected air travel and commercial real estate.

Political Influences Political influences include those that indirectly affect sector constituents, such as changes in trade, fiscal and monetary policies, regulations, and geopolitical factors, as well as direct government purchase or sale of an industry’s goods and services. In some industries, government-owned or controlled industry participants are common, which increases the potential effect of political factors on competitive analysis. For example, basic commodity producers or utilities are often owned or controlled by governments, such as oil producers Saudi Aramco and PetroChina; electricity producers, including Électricité de France SA (EDF); or mining companies, including National Copper Corporation of Chile (Codelco). In many cases, although industries may be dominated by privately held or publicly listed companies, the existence or potential threat of changes in government regulations, restrictions, or taxes may adversely impact future revenue and profitability. In contrast, subsidies or reimbursement of costs or fees associated with a product or service can improve an industry’s prospects or cause customers to favor one product over another. For example, governments in the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union offer consumers direct tax incentives for purchasing new electric vehicles and indirect tax incentives for driving EVs given that their use of electricity is not subject to national gasoline taxes, as in the case of cars with traditional internal combustion engines. As described earlier, governments often closely regulate the health care industry through the licensing of medical facilities and physicians but also through the reimbursement of medication costs under state-sponsored programs. The degree to which pharmaceutical drug costs are reimbursed by government agencies can be a key driver of product revenues, as described in the following example.
Example 18

Government Regulations and Pharmaceutical Industry Revenue The timing of release and the revenue and profitability potential of new drugs often hinge on government regulations, as described in the previous examples concerning Pfizer Inc. and Novo Nordisk A/S. Pfizer’s cholesterol-lowering statin drug, Lipitor, was developed in a multiphase government-sanctioned trial before receiving official approval for use in combating coronary heart disease. While under exclusive patent protection, US government health care agencies, such as Medicaid, covered the cost of Lipitor given its proven efficacy in lowering cholesterol and continue to reimburse the expense of low-cost generic versions of the drug. Novo Nordisk A/S developed its patented drug Ozempic and received official approval for its use to treat type 2 diabetes in 2017. Its subsequent approval at higher doses as a weight loss drug in 2021 held promise for many non-diabetic patients struggling with obesity. However, Medicaid and other US health care

agencies limited their Ozempic reimbursement to the treatment of diabetes only for the first several years of patent protection, constraining Novo Nordisk’s revenue and earnings potential for the drug.

Economic Influences Economic influences include short-term effects of economic fluctuations and long-term growth trends and structural changes that affect industry dynamics. Industry and competitive analysis must take the expected level of growth and inflation into consideration. The industry’s expected future performance should be consistent with these expectations, with adjustments based on whether an industry is considered to be defensive, cyclical, or in an above-trend growth phase. The influence of economic factors extends to longer-term trends, such as an economy’s stage of development and its competitiveness. As described in an earlier Economics learning module, developing countries attract capital investment, which increases labor productivity, leading to growth rates that exceed those of developed countries. Shifts in productive capacity from developed to developing markets lead many goods-producing industries to transfer mass production to low-wage countries, while service industries often take advantage of business process outsourcing (BPO), as described in the following example.
Example 19

BPO in the Philippines As one of the fastest growing economies in Southeast Asia, the Philippines has rapidly become a large provider of business process outsourcing activities, which exceeded USD35 billion in 2023 revenue and employed 1.7 million Filipinos. Key industries that take advantage of BPO include financial services, health care, and e-commerce firms. For example, US-based companies, such as JPMorgan Chase & Co., United Healthcare Group Inc., and Amazon.com, use BPO operations in the Philippines for customer service and back-office processing, often cutting the operational costs of such tasks in half by relocating tasks from domestic workers to this low-cost jurisdiction.

Exchange rates also influence industry growth and profitability by affecting both costs and the competitiveness of exports versus imports. When a domestic currency depreciates relative to other currencies, the cost of inputs, such as raw materials and energy, rises, reducing industry profit margins unless firms have a high degree of pricing power and are able to pass these costs on to consumers. Currency depreciation also boosts export competitiveness by making domestically produced goods and services less expensive for foreign buyers.

Social Influences Cultural and consumer trends, demographic changes, and changes in lifestyles or attitudes in a population are among the most important social influences that can affect industry growth and profitability. In some cases, social influences arise as a result of economic changes. For example, developing countries with rising levels of per capita GDP typically experience significant changes in consumer demand, shifting from a focus on low-cost necessities among consumers with little discretionary income to greater demand for higher-quality,

brand-name products. Rising per capita income levels drive increased demand for durable goods, such as appliances, furniture, and automobiles, as well as growth in spending on leisure, entertainment, and travel. Product differentiation in developed economies often focuses on quality, brand image, and features that tend to cater to diverse consumer preferences rather than solely competing on price. These features may include convenience, flexibility, or health consciousness but may also include transparency and disclosures surrounding product origin, including the local sourcing of inputs or the socially responsible procurement of raw materials using fair labor practices and safe working conditions. Industries and firms that are able to cater to local tastes, social trends, and cultural differences across markets are best able to combine steady growth in developed markets with more rapid expansion in developing markets. For example, restaurant franchising chains, such as McDonald’s Corporation and Subway IP LLC, adapt their menus to local tastes and locally source ingredients and dishes in order to broaden their appeal.

Technological Influences Technological change can result in the creation of new products or services, transform business models, and provide incremental improvements for existing industries or render existing offerings obsolete. As a key driver of total factor productivity for the overall economy and within an industry, analysts should consider when and how technological change will affect competition within a sector. It is useful to classify different forms of technological advancement based on their impact on a specific domain or sector and the problem or issue they are designed to address. A domain refers to an area in which an innovation is applied, which may include a product, business process, or specific market segment. While an innovation’s scope is defined by its domain, it may address a problem that can be directly translated into a new product or service or offer a less distinct solution without immediate commercial application. These types of technological advancements are often categorized on the basis of a so-called innovation matrix, as shown in Exhibit 12.

Starting from the bottom left quadrant of Exhibit 12, basic research involves developing an understanding of fundamental scientific principles that typically have no immediate commercial application. Basic research often builds a foundation for future innovation, and while governments and universities are often the largest sources of

basic science funding, companies in information technology, manufacturing, and the pharmaceutical industry commonly fund such research through grants or directly conduct research to advance product development. For example, in the field of medicine, laboratory experiments or animal testing may be used to determine the efficacy of a specific compound, which must be replicated and further assessed for harmful side effects before experimental use on humans. Pharmaceutical companies, such as Pfizer and Novo Nordisk, seek to capitalize on successful basic research by initiating early-stage clinical trials of medications that may receive approval for widespread use. Despite the large scale of basic research, commercial application of the results to generate revenue is typically years in the making and far from certain. Breakthrough innovation involves technology that establishes a new product, service, or business model or fundamentally changes existing businesses with a significant effect across industries. A prominent example of breakthrough innovation is the development of the rechargeable lithium-ion battery. Following years of basic materials research, the first commercialization of the technology took place in the early 1990s. Continued refinement of the technology, including improved energy density, battery life, and safety features, paved the way for its widespread adoption in smartphones, computers, power tools, and automobiles. Innovations with the most immediate financial impact on industries, products, and business models include sustaining innovations and disruptive innovations. Sustaining innovations are improvements in product or service performance and the addition of marginal features without a fundamental change in functionality or operation. These innovations are often led by industry incumbents, making improvements to better serve existing or adjacent customers’ needs. Successive improvements to reduce rechargeable lithium-ion battery size and prolong battery life in smartphones and automobiles represent sustaining innovations. Disruptive innovations are changes that create a new market or redefine an existing one with a different value proposition that may not immediately appeal to existing customers who are satisfied with the existing offering. While industry incumbents may lead disruptive innovation, it also provides an opportunity for entrants to rapidly capture market share. For example, the existing cable television industry was disrupted by streaming video delivered over the internet. While streaming technology was at first a rudimentary offering that appealed to consumers without cable subscriptions, it eventually grew to overtake cable in the number of subscribers. New entrants have relatively little at stake when pursuing a disruptive innovation because they do not have an existing profitable business to protect. As for incumbents, they can either invest in the disruptive innovation themselves—accelerating the decline of their existing business to maintain or grow market share—or ignore or more slowly adopt the innovative technology and lose market share, while continuing to generate strong profits in the near or medium term.

Legal Influences Legal influences on an industry include changes in laws and regulations from courts and policymakers that impose constraints or costs on industry participants, alter an industry’s business practices or economic outcomes, or fundamentally change an industry’s growth and profitability prospects by either banning or allowing certain activities. These influences may either promote or constrain business activity in one jurisdiction versus another, causing firms to move or outsource certain operations or target growth in areas with fewer legal restrictions, as described in the following example.
Example 20

Regulatory Constraints and the Global Pharmaceutical Industry As described in earlier Pfizer Inc. and Novo Nordisk A/S examples, the global pharmaceutical industry is tightly regulated. Firms introducing new medications must go through a series of clinical trial protocols and extensive new drug approval processes from agencies including the US Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in the European Union. While the FDA and EMA approval processes differ, both are focused on the highest health and safety standards for new medications when granting intellectual property protection, such as patents. Given its competitive advantage in terms of relatively low production costs, a highly skilled workforce, and local government policies that promote generic drug use, the Indian pharmaceutical industry rapidly developed by specializing in reducing the prices of drugs that are no longer under patent protection through the local manufacture of active pharmaceutical ingredients. As a result, India supplies over 20% of the world’s generic drugs, with a US generic drug market share of over 40%. Differing pharmaceutical industry regulatory and legal regimes have played a key role in the development of the industry in India. For example, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, a multinational drug company based in Hyderabad, India, began as a domestic supplier to Indian drug manufacturers, later expanding operations to export medications to unregulated markets. As the company grew, it established FDA-approved facilities in India that manufactured active pharmaceutical ingredients. In 2001, Dr. Reddy’s became the first Indian company to launch a generic drug in the United States, and it listed its public shares in the United States during the same year. Since that time, the company has continued to expand in Europe and the United States through acquisitions and partnerships in order to conduct clinical trials and develop new drugs.

Examples of industries strongly affected by legal influences include tobacco and cannabis. Developed economies have imposed wide-ranging laws and restrictions on the manufacturing, distribution, marketing, sale, and use of tobacco products to discourage consumption and the associated adverse health consequences. Because most of the legal constraints on consumption focus on high cigarette taxes and smoking bans in public places, tobacco companies have adapted by increasing their offerings of smokeless tobacco products, with over a third of industry revenue generated by these alternative offerings. In contrast to the tobacco industry, the legalization of cannabis represents an evolving legal environment in which some markets, such as Canada and Germany, have legalized its production, sale, and use. Other markets, such as the United States, have varying laws at the local level, while it remains a controlled and illegal substance in most Asian jurisdictions. Given both the social stigma and the well-publicized negative health effects of smoking in many developed markets, cannabis industry offerings have rapidly evolved to include edible products, which represent a growing proportion of overall cannabis industry revenues. The examples of the pharmaceutical, tobacco, and cannabis industries demonstrate how industries evolve and adapt to legal constraints and a changing legal environment over time. Legal factors are intertwined with technological influences in cases where innovations occur with no established legal framework or precedent.

For example, a key area of sustained innovation in the automotive industry involves the introduction of autonomous driver assistance features. These include speed control, autonomous steering and acceleration, and environmental detection capabilities using a combination of cameras, radar, and lidar technology. However, the introduction of fully autonomous vehicles with no human intervention remains experimental in many countries and is subject to legal limitations, as described next.
Example 21

Self-Driving Cars and the Legal Landscape Although many automakers have developed various levels of driver-assisted technology, the use of fully automated vehicles (AVs), where all driving tasks are performed without human intervention, remains at an experimental stage. While no widely accepted global regulatory AV framework exists, as in the case of the Geneva Convention on Road Traffic, signed by over 100 countries, many governments seek to establish uniform rules surrounding operational responsibility, safety standards, software reliability, environmental performance, and cybersecurity, as well as the protection of people and property outside the AV. While no formal nationwide AV laws exist in the Chinese Mainland as of 2024, the Ministry of Public Security has established 32,000 km of roads for AV testing and 16,000 test licenses, with 20 cities testing autonomous taxis and buses. In the case of Australia, existing legal barriers prohibited full AV operation on public roads in 2024, although updated regulations are under discussion. The EU passed legislation in 2022 establishing a legal framework for the approval of automated and fully driverless vehicles, with each country slated to create its own legislation. Germany’s first trial of highly automated self-driving taxis began on public roads in mid-2024. While no uniform US federal law on AVs was in place as of 2024, several US states, including Nevada and Arizona, initiated local legislation allowing the early adoption of autonomous vehicles on a limited scale.

Environmental Influences Environmental influences on industry and competitive analysis are often closely associated with political, social, and/or legal influences. Energy producers and heavy consumers of energy are among the industries whose growth and profitability are most heavily impacted by environmental factors. A key question for energy producers involves the risks and opportunities associated with the so-called energy transition, or structural shift mandated by many global governments to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases in overall energy use. As national governments implement energy policy changes at varying speeds and with different combinations of taxes and subsidies, industry participants take different approaches in adapting to incentives and expected policy changes, as described in the following example.
Example 22

RWE AG and Enel S.p.A. Approaches to the Energy Transition Germany-based RWE AG and Italian utility Enel S.p.A. are multinational firms that represent the largest electric utilities in their domestic markets. While both firms are focused on increasing renewable energy capacity and reducing fossil fuel emissions in alignment with European Union policies, their strategies reflect the unique regulatory, tax, and subsidy policies of their respective countries. RWE AG has committed to invest over EUR50 billion in renewable technologies through 2030, 40% of which is slated for onshore wind and solar projects, 35% for offshore wind, and the remainder for hydrogen and battery technology. Germany’s Energiewende transition policy prioritizes the phaseout of both coal and nuclear power in part by subsidizing investment in power plants that may be converted to hydrogen. In contrast, around the same time, Enel S.p.A. committed to investing EUR43billion over a three-year period in its grid networks and renewable projects. Around 60% of Enel’s total investment is to be allocated to the improvement and expansion of its electricity grids to accommodate sources of renewable energy. Enel’s investment strategy seeks to promote infrastructure digitalization to make electricity distribution more efficient, with the goal of equipping 80% of its customers with smart meters by 2025.

Transition risks and opportunities are of similar importance for industries representing energy consumers, such as airlines, global shipping, the automotive industry, and other manufacturing industries that are users of fossil fuels responsible for carbon emissions. Changes in regulations, taxes, and/or consumer preferences will continue to lead companies in these sectors to evolve their business operations or face market share losses to competing solutions with lower carbon emissions.

1. Which of the following represents the prevention of the threat to industry entrants for an indefinite period? A. Patent protection B. Licensing requirements C. Proprietary technology Solution: C is correct because the existence of proprietary technology can prevent the threat of entry only as long as other potential market participants fail to replicate a company’s technology. A is incorrect because patent protection provides a competitive advantage by preventing industry entry for a finite period of time. B is incorrect because licensing requirements provide a competitive advantage for a specific period of time.

2. Which of the following set of factors is most likely to lead to greater bargaining power among an industry’s suppliers? A. Higher concentration of available suppliers, more tailored inputs, and high switching costs

B. Lower concentration of suppliers, less tailored inputs, and higher switching costs C. Higher concentration of suppliers, more tailored inputs, and lower switching costs Solution: A is correct because more concentrated suppliers, more tailored inputs, and high switching costs lead to higher supplier bargaining power. B is incorrect because less concentrated suppliers and more standard inputs reduce supplier bargaining power. C is incorrect because low switching costs reduce supplier bargaining power.

3. Which of the following forms of innovation represents technology that establishes a new product or changes businesses with a significant effect across industries? A. Breakthrough innovation B. Sustaining innovation C. Disruptive innovation Solution: A is correct because breakthrough innovation involves a new product, service, or business model that may fundamentally change existing businesses across multiple industries. B is incorrect because sustaining innovation involves incremental technological improvements often led by industry incumbents that improves existing products or services. C is incorrect because disruptive innovation can create a new market or enter an existing one with a different value proposition.

• Analysts apply industry and competitive analysis to define and identify value drivers, competitive forces, and external factors affecting groups of companies that offer similar products and services to their customers.

• The first step in conducting industry and competitive analysis is to classify an industry and its constituents, whether using third-party classification schemes or other criteria, such as geography.

• Once the scope of an industry is established, an industry survey, including overall size, growth, and profitability and covering the competitive landscape, provides a basis for further assessment. Industry dynamics may be compared to economic trends to determine the industry’s stage in the life cycle, business cycle sensitivity, and level of competitive rivalry, including market shares and trends of key industry participants.

• Porter’s Five Forces provide a framework to analyze an industry’s structure as defined by the level of competitive rivalry. Key factors include the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, and customer and supplier bargaining power. These forces may be evaluated based on the width of an economic moat, which is affected by intangible assets, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, or efficient scale within an industry or among firms.
• PESTLE analysis is conducted to assess the effect of political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental factors on an industry’s prospective growth rate and market share dynamics.

1. Which of the following statements best describes the characteristics of growth companies? A. Unlike defensive or cyclical companies, growth companies tend to exhibit smaller revenue declines in an economic downturn.
B. Unlike defensive or cyclical companies, growth companies tend to exhibit higher profitability during economic expansion.
C. Unlike defensive or cyclical companies, growth companies exhibit higher revenue growth independent of economic fluctuations.

2. Which of the following statements provides the best justification for grouping companies using a geographic rather than industry approach? A. Firms that face similar economic conditions in the same country may have more common value drivers than those in the same industry.
B. Firms listed on the same exchange may have more common value drivers than those in the same industry.
C. Firms that report financial statements in the same currency may have more common value drivers than those in the same industry.

3. Which of the following statements best describes the challenges of using a bottom-up approach to measure industry size? A. A bottom-up approach is difficult to apply when government statistics for a specific sector are unavailable.
B. A bottom-up approach is difficult to apply when an industry classification involves a strict hierarchical taxonomy.
C. A bottom-up approach is difficult to apply when an industry includes a large proportion of private companies or small businesses.

4. Which of the following statements best describes third-party industry classification schemes? A. Third-party classification schemes combine companies with a similar business model into the same industry.
B. Third-party classification schemes align companies to a single industry that represents their primary operating activity.
C. Third-party classification schemes assign the different activities of companies operating across industries to each of their different industries.

5. Which of the following statements best describes the use of vertical integration as a competitive strategy? A. Vertical integration may be used to expand operations into an earlier stage of production to offset supplier bargaining power.
B. Vertical integration may be used to outsource production to offset consumer bargaining power.
C. Vertical integration may be used to expand operations in order to reduce the threat of substitutes for an industry’s products or services.

6. Which of the following statements best describes the contrast between the impacts of basic research and sustaining innovation on an industry? A. Basic research involves developing an understanding of scientific principles, while sustaining innovation aims to minimize a firm’s environmental impact.
B. Basic research creates new industries, while sustaining innovation fundamentally changes existing businesses across multiple industries.
C. Basic research generally has no immediate commercial application, while sustaining innovation involves incremental improvements to existing products or services.
7. Which of the following sets of industry circumstances minimizes the threat of entry? A. A greater proportion of intangible assets, lower network effects, and lower switching costs
B. A lower proportion of intangible assets, greater cost advantages, and less efficient scale
C. A greater proportion of intangible assets, higher network effects, and higher switching costs
8. Which of the following statements is consistent with lower industry concentration? A. Lower industry concentration is consistent with a higher Herfindahl– Hirschman Index.
B. Lower industry concentration is generally consistent with greater competitive intensity.
C. Lower industry concentration is generally consistent with lower product differentiation.
Solutions

1. C is correct because growth company performance is relatively insensitive to the business cycle. A is incorrect because the revenue of growth companies is typically less related to economic cycles. B is incorrect because growth companies exhibit higher revenue growth, which may or may not be accompanied by high profitability.

2. A is correct because companies operating within a jurisdiction may have more common value drivers due to political, economic, and social policies and conditions than those operating in various jurisdictions within an industry. B is incorrect because operating within the same industry typically results in more common value drivers relative to listing on a common exchange. C is incorrect because operating within the same industry results in more common value drivers relative to having the same reporting currency.

3. C is correct because it is more difficult to estimate revenue for private companies or small businesses than to access disclosures for large, publicly listed companies. B is incorrect because strict hierarchical taxonomies are not a challenge specific to a bottom-up approach to estimating industry size. A is incorrect because the lack of government statistics for a sector is a challenge for a top-down—not a bottom-up—approach to estimating industry size.

4. B is correct because third-party classification schemes are based on a strict hierarchical taxonomy that assigns each company to a single industry. A is incorrect because companies within the same industry may have different business models. C is incorrect because companies operating across industries are assigned to a single industry that represents a firm’s largest business activity.

5. A is correct because vertical integration may be used to offset supplier bargaining power by expanding production to an earlier stage. B is incorrect because vertical integration involves the insourcing rather than the outsourcing of production processes. C is incorrect because vertical integration does not address the threat of substitutes for a company’s products or services.

6. C is correct because basic research involves discoveries with no immediate commercial impact, while sustaining innovation makes small improvements to existing products or services. A is incorrect because sustaining innovation does not necessarily address a product’s environmental impact. B is incorrect because basic research generally requires longer periods until commercialization, while breakthrough innovation fundamentally changes existing businesses across multiple industries.

7. C is correct because more intangible assets, higher network effects, and higher switching costs all represent barriers to entry. A is incorrect because higher, not lower, network effects and switching costs deter industry entrants. B is incorrect because higher, not lower, intangible assets and more efficient scale are factors limiting industry entrants.

8. B is correct because lower industry concentration involves many industry participants supplying a good or service, which generally leads to higher competitive intensity. A is incorrect because lower industry concentration is consistent with a lower, not higher, Herfindahl–Hirschman Index. C is incorrect because product differentiation is not determined by the degree of industry concentration.

evaluate a company’s revenue drivers, operating profitability, and pricing power
evaluate a company’s working capital, capital investments, and capital structure

blocks.x: PRESENT, AND FUTURE | 1

This learning module builds on prior industry and competitive analysis by focusing on an individual company’s strategy and positioning. Financial analysts must gain a thorough understanding of these elements in order to explain the key drivers of a company’s operating, investing, and financing activities in the past, as well as the present and future. These factors support the evaluation of company performance using income statement and balance sheet metrics. A thorough company analysis provides critical context for company valuation and serves as a key component of a comprehensive equity research report. In the second lesson, we address a firm’s market and pricing strategy and its competitive position within an industry. The firm’s business model and its addressable market, its current stage in the company life cycle, and the size of its economic moat as described in the prior learning module are important elements in this analysis. Next, we turn our focus to how these factors affect a firm’s income statement, including revenue drivers, pricing power, and operating profitability and its balance sheet dynamics, including investments in assets and debt and equity financing. This analysis provides a narrative to substantiate revenue and earnings forecasts as introduced in an earlier learning module, allowing analysts to support an investment recommendation and intrinsic value estimate for a specific company in an equity research report.

sections.title: Pre-Test: Company Analysis: Past, Present, And Future

blocks.x: 1. Compared to a firm’s serviceable addressable market, its obtainable addressable market is further constrained by the company’s: A. focus. B. scale. C. geographic presence. Solution: B is correct. B is correct because a firm’s serviceable addressable market depends only upon a firm’s focus and geographic presence, while its obtainable addressable market is further constrained by the firm’s current scale and strategy. A is incorrect because a firm’s serviceable market also depends on its focus. C is incorrect because a firm’s serviceable market also depends on its geographic presence.

2. Cost leadership strategies are most common for: A. startup companies. B. differentiated products. C. commoditized products. Solution: C is correct. C is correct because cost leadership strategies can offer companies an attractive competitive strategy when little to no differentiation exists among competitor products. A is incorrect because startup companies are commonly establishing a business model with little to no revenue and negative cash flow and are usually not in the position to feasibly establish cost leadership. B is incorrect because a lack of commoditization within an industry is more likely to lead to differentiation strategies than cost leadership.

3. A firm is most likely to have pricing power if it: A. supplies price-elastic goods. B. supplies price-inelastic goods. C. uses price-elastic goods as inputs. Solution: B is correct. B is correct because price-inelastic goods are those for which changes in price have little effect on demand, increasing the pricing power of firms who supply them. A is incorrect because price-elastic goods are those for which changes in price have a greater effect on demand, lowering the pricing power of firms who supply them. C is incorrect because using price-elastic goods as inputs has an indeterminate effect on a firm’s pricing power.

4. Which of the following is most likely an example of a top-down approach to company revenue analysis? A. The firm’s geographic sales distribution. B. The firm’s product mix. C. The firm’s market share within an industry. Solution: C is correct. C is correct because the economy, the firm’s industry, and the firm’s market share reflect top-down approaches to analyzing company revenue. A is incorrect, as a firm’s geographic sales distribution represents a bottom-up, not a top-down, approach to company revenue analysis. B is incorrect, as a firm’s product mix represents a bottom-up, not a topdown, approach to company revenue analysis.

5. A shorter cash conversion cycle implies that a company: A. has more working capital. B. pays its suppliers more quickly. C. efficiently manages inventory and receivables while obtaining favorable payment terms from suppliers. Solution: C is correct. C is correct because the cash conversion cycle is equal to days of inventory on hand plus days sales outstanding less days payable outstanding. Shorter cash conversion cycles therefore involve minimizing inventory and collection periods while maximizing the time to meet payable obligations. A is incorrect because a shorter cash conversion cycle implies less, not more, working capital. B is incorrect, as more quickly meeting payment obligations to suppliers does not shorten but rather lengthens the cash conversion cycle.

6. In a given year, a company can increase its free cash flow to equity (FCFE) by increasing its: A. debt. B. working capital. C. capital expenditures. Solution: A is correct. A is correct because an increase in debt is considered a cash flow to shareholders. A company’s FCFE is equal to cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures plus net debt issuance. B is incorrect, as an increase in working capital is a use of funds that lowers cash flow from operations and reduces FCFE. C is incorrect, as increasing capital expenditures reduces FCFE.
POSITION
explain a company’s competitive strategy and position within an industry

An earlier Corporate Finance learning module described how companies create value via their business model, which includes the firm’s existing and prospective customers, products or services offered to those customers, key resources and assets used by the business, as well as its key partners and suppliers. A firm’s competitive strategy is a key determinant of its business model. All firms have a competitive strategy, whether intentional or not. An intentional strategy is one which informs the company’s business model, sets measurable goals communicated internally and externally to investors, tracks performance and incorporates a feedback loop to refine and improve the company’s future strategy. An unintentional strategy results from managers pursuing their own incentives, repeating whatever was done in the past, or simply copying industry leaders or professional norms. Companies with effective strategies are more likely to create value for their investors. While public stock prices may reflect perceptions about value creation, it is difficult to correctly judge value creation until time has passed. To evaluate competitive strategies on a forward-looking basis, analysts should consider three dimensions:
• How well does the strategy defend the firm against Porter’s Five Forces?
• Is the strategy aligned with, or at least not in conflict with, external industry factors identified in a PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental) analysis?

• Does the firm have the resources and capabilities to execute the strategy? The ability of individual firms to create value on a sustained basis is influenced by the company and industry’s stage of development, a company’s reaction to the competitive dynamics within its industry, as well as the external influences that shape its operating environment.

Competitive Strategies for Startups, Growth Companies, and Firms in Decline A company’s competitive strategy and positioning varies significantly over the company life cycle. As described in earlier Corporate Finance learning modules, firms are commonly categorized by their life-cycle stage as shown in Exhibit 1. We first address strategic implications for startups, growth firms, and firms in decline in this section of the lesson and devote the remainder of the lesson to mature firms.
Exhibit 1: Company Life-Cycle Stages

Startup companies usually involve firms with little or no revenue, negative cash flow, and few assets, while growth companies often transition to profitability and exhibit above-trend revenue and earnings growth. Given the limited operating history of these firms, analysts must rely on factors beyond historical performance when conducting company analysis. In the earliest stage of development, a company’s primary focus is often to establish a business model. When engaged in new product development, a startup firm must create a prototype or otherwise establish the ability to address an unmet customer need. These firms face a very high level of risk and likelihood of failure as illustrated in the following example.
Example 1

BioAge Labs’ Obesity Drug Innovation An earlier Equities learning module described the application of Porter’s Five Forces in the health care industry’s product development of diabetes and obesity solutions due to the success of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk’s patented weight-loss drug that generated nearly USD17 billion of revenue in 2024. One example of an early-stage company is BioAge Labs Inc. (BIOA), a US-based biotechnology firm. Unlike large health care firms such as Eli Lilly or Pfizer with existing products, the company had no existing products or revenue, focusing solely on clinical development of new therapies for obesity and metabolic diseases. In early trials, BioAge Labs’ leading oral compound azelaprag showed promise in enhancing muscle metabolism, reducing muscle atrophy, and maintaining fitness among sedentary subjects. This initial success led to several rounds of private equity funding followed by an IPO in September 2024.
